front: Why is power transmitted over long distances at high voltage?
back: For the same power, current falls as voltage rises, so I²R line losses fall roughly with 1/V².
explain: Power P = √3·V·I·cosφ; doubling voltage halves current for the same power, cutting resistive losses to a quarter. This is why generation at 11–33 kV is stepped up for transmission and stepped down at substations, whose main role is voltage transformation. HVDC is preferred for very long distances because it avoids reactive power flow and has lower losses there.

front: A plant receives 96 MU at its end and the T&D efficiency is 80%. How much generation is required?
explain: Energy delivered = energy generated × T&D efficiency, so generation = delivered ÷ efficiency. A common trap is to multiply (96 × 0.8 = 76.8) instead of dividing. The 24 MU difference is the T&D loss.

front: How is the AT&C (Aggregate Technical & Commercial) loss of a distribution utility calculated?
back: AT&C loss = 1 − (Billing efficiency × Collection efficiency).
explain: Billing efficiency = energy billed (metered + unmetered assessed) ÷ input energy. Collection efficiency = amount actually collected for current bills (excluding arrears) ÷ amount billed. Example: billing 80% and collection 75% gives AT&C loss = 1 − 0.6 = 40%. Revenue realised per kWh input = current collections ÷ input energy.

front: What makes up a two-part industrial electricity tariff?
back: A demand charge (on contract or recorded maximum demand, Rs/kVA or Rs/kW per month) plus an energy charge (Rs/kWh).
explain: The demand charge recovers the utility's fixed capacity cost, the energy charge its running cost. Many tariffs add power-factor incentives or penalties and Time-of-Day (ToD) rates. Lowering MD and improving PF therefore cut the bill even when kWh is unchanged.

front: What is the purpose of a Time-of-Day (ToD) tariff?
back: To shift consumption from peak hours to off-peak hours by charging more for peak energy and less for off-peak energy.
explain: Utilities face their highest purchase cost at the evening peak. Consumers can save by rescheduling flexible loads (pumping, batch processes, thermal or ice storage) to night. A DISCOM can also pay incentives for load shifting: net saving = (peak cost − off-peak cost − incentive) × kWh shifted.

front: How is Maximum Demand (MD) recorded by a utility meter?
back: As the highest average kVA (or kW) over any demand integration interval in the billing month, typically 15 or 30 minutes.
explain: Because MD is an average over the interval, a short motor-start spike matters less than sustained simultaneous loading. MD can be reduced by staggering loads, load shedding with an MD controller, rescheduling non-critical loads, using captive generation at peak, and improving PF (which lowers kVA for the same kW).

front: Define load factor and explain why a high load factor is desirable.
back: Load factor = average load ÷ maximum demand over a period. A high load factor spreads the fixed demand charge over more kWh, lowering the average cost per unit.
explain: Average load = kWh consumed ÷ hours in the period. For example, 2,00,000 kWh in a 720-hour month with MD 500 kW gives load factor = 277.8/500 = 55.6%. Flattening the load profile raises load factor and lets the same supply infrastructure serve more energy.

front: What does a power factor of unity mean?
back: No reactive power (kVAr) is drawn from the supply; kVA equals kW and current is in phase with voltage.
explain: Power factor = kW/kVA = cos φ. Inductive loads such as motors and transformers draw lagging magnetising current, so PF is below 1. At unity PF the supply current is the minimum possible for the given real power.

front: What is the formula for the capacitor kVAr needed to raise PF from cos φ1 to cos φ2?
back: kVAr = kW × (tan φ1 − tan φ2).
explain: The real power (kW) stays the same; only the reactive component is reduced. Find φ = cos⁻¹(PF) for each PF and take the tangent. Multiplier tables in BEE books list (tan φ1 − tan φ2) directly; for example, 0.75 → 0.95 gives 0.553.

front: How does a capacitor bank improve the power factor?
back: It supplies leading reactive power locally, offsetting the lagging kVAr drawn by inductive loads, so less kVAr (and current) comes from the supply.
explain: The capacitor does not change the kW of the load. The net kVAr seen upstream of the capacitor falls, so kVA and current fall. That releases transformer and cable capacity, reduces I²R losses and improves voltage.

front: If the tail-end power factor is improved from 0.80 to 0.95, by what percentage do distribution (I²R) losses fall?
back: About 29%. Losses scale with 1/PF², so the reduction = 1 − (0.80/0.95)² = 0.29.
explain: For constant kW and voltage, current ∝ 1/PF, so I²R losses ∝ 1/PF². New losses = (0.8/0.95)² ≈ 0.709 of the original. Capacitors deliver this saving only on the network upstream of where they are connected, so installing them at the load (tail) end maximises the loss reduction.

front: A plant draws 500 kW at 0.75 PF lagging. It installs capacitors to raise the PF to 0.95. Find the capacitor kVAr needed, the kVA demand before and after, and the percentage reduction in distribution losses upstream of the capacitors.
back: Capacitor ≈ 277 kVAr; kVA falls from 666.7 to 526.3 (≈ 140 kVA MD reduction); upstream I²R losses fall by ≈ 37.7%.
explain: PF correction leaves kW unchanged and removes reactive kVAr, so kVA and current both fall. Because losses scale with the square of the current, a 21% current reduction gives about a 38% loss reduction. This calculation underlies every 'MD reduction by PF improvement' question.

The demand charge is billed on kVA, so this reduction cuts the monthly bill directly.

front: What are the two main types of transformer loss, and how does each vary with load?
back: No-load (core/iron) loss is roughly constant whenever the transformer is energised. Load (copper, I²R) loss varies with the square of the load.
explain: Core loss is hysteresis plus eddy-current loss in the laminations and depends on voltage and frequency, not load. Copper loss at x per-unit load = x² × full-load copper loss. Total loss = NL + x²·FL_Cu. A lightly loaded transformer is therefore dominated by its core loss.

front: A 750 kVA transformer has 1200 W no-load loss and 7200 W full-load copper loss. What is its total loss at 60% load?
explain: Only the copper loss is scaled, and by the square of the load fraction. A common error is to scale it linearly (giving 5520 W).

front: At what load does a transformer reach maximum efficiency?
back: When copper (load) loss equals core (no-load) loss, at a per-unit load of √(No-load loss / Full-load copper loss).
explain: For NL = 1.8 kW and FL Cu = 10.5 kW, the maximum efficiency occurs at √(1.8/10.5) = 0.414, i.e. about 41% load. Distribution transformers are designed for peak efficiency at part load because they spend much time lightly loaded.

front: What do amorphous-core transformers mainly reduce?
back: No-load (core) losses.
explain: Amorphous metal has very low hysteresis loss and high resistivity (low eddy currents), so core loss is far below that of CRGO steel. They suit distribution transformers that stay energised 24 hours a day at low average load. Load (copper) losses are not inherently reduced.

front: A 1000 kVA transformer has 1.8 kW no-load loss and 10.5 kW full-load copper loss. It supplies 600 kVA at 0.9 PF for 24 h/day. Find the total loss, the efficiency at this load, the load for maximum efficiency, and the daily energy lost.
back: Loss = 5.58 kW; efficiency ≈ 98.98%; maximum efficiency at ≈ 414 kVA (41.4% load); daily loss ≈ 134 kWh.
explain: Part-load transformer losses use the 'NL + x²·FL_Cu' rule. Maximum efficiency occurs where the variable loss equals the fixed loss. Even at 99% efficiency, the losses are worth tracking because they accumulate every hour of the year.

steps.explain: Copper loss ∝ (load)².
Core loss is constant.

front: Which loads generate harmonics? Give examples.
back: Non-linear loads that draw non-sinusoidal current, such as VFDs and inverters, UPS, rectifiers, SMPS, LED or CFL drivers, arc furnaces and welding sets.
explain: A VFD or inverter drive is a far larger harmonic source than an LED lamp, transformer or resistance heater (a resistance heater is linear). Harmonic currents are integer multiples of the 50 Hz fundamental (250 Hz is the 5th harmonic, and so on).

front: What problems do harmonics cause in an electrical system?
back: Overheating of transformers, cables and motors; overloaded neutrals from triplen harmonics; capacitor failure from resonance; nuisance tripping; meter errors; interference with electronics.
explain: Harmonics increase RMS current without adding useful power, which raises I²R and eddy losses. Third-order (triplen) harmonics add in the neutral of 3-phase, 4-wire systems instead of cancelling. Capacitor banks can resonate with system inductance at a harmonic frequency.

front: What is the effect of voltage unbalance between the three phases on an induction motor?
back: It causes negative-sequence currents that greatly increase current unbalance, losses and winding temperature, reducing efficiency and motor life.
explain: A small voltage unbalance (a few percent) produces a current unbalance several times larger, because the motor's negative-sequence impedance is low. The extra heating can force derating. Causes include unequal single-phase loads and blown capacitor fuses, so balance single-phase loads across phases.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q30 / BEE 2025 P3 Q23

front: What is the formula for the synchronous speed of an induction motor?
back: Ns = 120 f / P (rpm), where f = supply frequency and P = number of poles. It is inversely proportional to the number of poles.
explain: At 50 Hz: 2 pole = 3000 rpm, 4 pole = 1500 rpm, 6 pole = 1000 rpm, 8 pole = 750 rpm. The rotor runs slightly slower than Ns; that difference (slip) is what induces rotor current and torque.

front: A 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 1470 rpm. What is its slip?
explain: Ns = 120 × 50 / 4 = 1500 rpm. Slip = (Ns − N)/Ns = (1500 − 1470)/1500 = 0.02. Slip rises roughly in proportion to load, which is the basis of the slip method of estimating motor loading.

front: List the five loss components of an induction motor.
back: Stator copper (I²R) loss, rotor copper loss, core (iron) loss, friction and windage loss, and stray load loss.
explain: Core loss and friction & windage are roughly fixed and independent of load. Stator and rotor copper losses vary with the square of the load current. Stray load losses arise mainly from leakage flux induced by load currents and also rise with load (roughly with the square of load torque, not inversely).

front: How do motor efficiency and power factor change at light load?
back: Both fall. Efficiency usually stays near its peak from about 50–100% load but drops sharply below about 40–50%. PF falls significantly as load decreases.
explain: At light load the fixed losses (core, friction) are a larger share of a small output, and the magnetising current (reactive) stays nearly constant while the active current falls. So the statement 'PF improves as load decreases' is false. Larger motors generally have higher full-load efficiency.

front: What is the formula for energy savings from replacing a motor with a more efficient one?
back: kW saved = kW output × (1/η_old − 1/η_new).
explain: Input = output/η, so the saving is the difference in input power for the same shaft output. Multiply by operating hours for kWh. Use efficiencies at the actual operating load, not nameplate, and check that the new motor's lower slip does not raise the load on centrifugal equipment.

front: How do energy-efficient (IE2/IE3) motors achieve higher efficiency?
back: By reducing losses: more copper and larger conductors (lower I²R), thinner low-loss electrical steel laminations (lower core loss), smaller and more efficient cooling fans, and optimised design with tight quality control.
explain: An IE3 motor's gain over IE2 comes mainly from reduced copper and iron losses, not from increased slip (EE motors actually have lower slip). Inrush current is not lower, and the saving is smallest at very light load.

front: Why can replacing a standard motor with a high-efficiency motor on a centrifugal pump or fan sometimes give less saving than expected?
back: EE motors have lower slip, so they run faster. Under the affinity laws, flow rises with speed and power with speed cubed, which eats into the efficiency gain.
explain: For example, if speed rises from 1460 to 1480 rpm, the pump flow rises about 1.4% and the shaft power about 4%. Compare kWh per unit of output (e.g. kWh per m³ pumped), not just kW, when validating savings.

front: What is the effect of running a lightly loaded delta-connected motor in star connection?
back: The phase voltage drops by √3, so the motor's capability falls to about one-third. At low load, iron losses fall and PF and efficiency improve.
explain: This is a low-cost measure for motors that run below about 40% load most of the time. The motor must never see more than its star-mode capability or it will overheat. Automatic star-delta changeover controllers switch modes based on load.

front: What does a soft starter do?
back: It ramps up the voltage during starting to limit inrush current and mechanical shock. It does not change full-load speed or improve running efficiency.
explain: Direct-on-line starting draws 6–8 times rated current. A soft starter uses thyristors to raise the voltage gradually, reducing voltage dips and stress on couplings and belts. Some models also provide energy-saving voltage reduction at light load.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q37 / BEE 2025 P3 Q24

front: In a VFD, what happens if the frequency is reduced while the voltage is kept the same?
back: The motor is over-fluxed: the magnetising current rises, and the motor draws higher current and may overheat.
explain: Air-gap flux ∝ V/f, so VFDs keep V/f constant (or use vector control) as speed falls. Keeping V constant while lowering f pushes the core into saturation.

front: How does motor operating temperature affect insulation life?
back: As a rule of thumb, insulation life roughly doubles for every 10°C reduction in operating temperature (and halves for every 10°C rise).
explain: This is why overloading, voltage unbalance, poor ventilation and frequent starts shorten motor life. EE motors run cooler because they have lower losses, which also extends their life.

front: A 37 kW, 415 V motor has nameplate current 65 A and PF 0.86. In the field it draws 48 A at 412 V and 0.82 PF. Estimate the rated efficiency and the present percentage loading.
back: Rated input ≈ 40.2 kW, rated efficiency ≈ 92.1%; actual input ≈ 28.1 kW, loading ≈ 70%.
explain: Nameplate V, I and PF give rated input power; rated output ÷ rated input is the rated efficiency. Comparing measured input with rated input gives the loading by the input-ratio method. Note that current alone is a poor indicator of load because PF also changes with load.

steps.explain: P = √3·V·I·PF.
η = rated output / rated input.

explain: Savings come from lower input power for the same shaft output. The formula kW_out × (1/η_old − 1/η_new) is a frequent one-mark question. In practice, confirm the shaft load stays the same: a lower-slip motor may speed up a centrifugal load.

front: How do you calculate the Free Air Delivery (FAD) from displacement and volumetric efficiency?
back: FAD = swept (displacement) volume × volumetric efficiency. For example, 150 CFM × 0.90 = 135 CFM.
explain: FAD is the actual air delivered, referred to inlet conditions. It is always below displacement because of clearance volume re-expansion, heating of intake air, valve losses and leakage past rings. Worn compressors show falling volumetric efficiency.

front: How is leakage estimated from a load/unload (on-off) test with all users closed?
back: Leakage = Compressor FAD × T / (T + t), where T = average on-load time and t = average unload time.
explain: Example: a 500 cfm compressor loading 5 s and unloading 20 s gives 500 × 5/25 = 100 cfm of leakage (20%). Several cycles are averaged. Leakage in well-maintained systems should be below about 5–10% of capacity.

front: What is the effect of intake air temperature on compressor power?
back: Cooler intake air reduces power. Each 4°C rise in intake temperature increases power consumption by about 1% for the same output.
explain: Cooler air is denser, so more mass is delivered per stroke or revolution. Drawing intake air from outside or a shaded, ventilated location rather than the hot compressor room is a standard energy-saving measure. Higher intake temperature therefore lowers efficiency.

front: What saving results from reducing compressor discharge pressure?
back: Roughly 6–10% of compressor power per 1 bar reduction, so generate air at the lowest pressure the users actually need.
explain: Higher pressure also increases leakage flow from every leak. Separate high-pressure users can be supplied by a small booster instead of running the whole system at high pressure.

front: At higher altitude, how does compressor power compare for the same FAD?
back: It consumes more power.
explain: At altitude the ambient pressure is lower, so the compression ratio to reach the same gauge pressure is higher. Less mass is drawn per stroke, so more work is needed per unit of free air delivered.

front: What do the intercooler and aftercooler do in a compressed air system?
back: The intercooler cools air between stages, bringing compression closer to isothermal and reducing work. The aftercooler cools the discharge air so that moisture condenses and can be drained.
explain: A fouled intercooler raises the second-stage inlet temperature and power. Proper aftercooling with automatic drain traps reduces the load on dryers and prevents water in the distribution lines.
source: BEE 2025 P3 Q15 / BEE 2024 P3 Q39

front: How do desiccant dryers work, and which dryer type usually has the lowest operating cost?
back: Desiccant dryers adsorb moisture on silica gel or activated alumina. Heat-of-compression dryers, which regenerate using the compressor's own hot discharge air, generally have the lowest operating energy.
explain: Heatless (purge) dryers lose about 15–20% of the dried air for regeneration, so their running cost is high. Refrigerated dryers are economical for moderate dew-point needs. Choose the highest dew point the process can accept.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q40 / BEE 2025 P3 Q45

front: What are the main features of screw, reciprocating and centrifugal compressors?
back: Screw: continuous, pulsation-free delivery, but poor efficiency at part load (unloaded running), so not ideal for fluctuating demand without VSD. Reciprocating: good part-load efficiency, pulsating flow. Centrifugal: large capacities, capacity controlled efficiently by inlet guide vanes.
explain: A VSD on a screw compressor eliminates unloaded running and matches output to demand. Typical practice is to run base-load units at full load and give the trim duty to one VSD or reciprocating unit.

front: List five energy conservation measures for a compressed air system.
back: Arrest leaks; reduce generation pressure; draw cool intake air; use VSD or proper capacity control and sequencing; eliminate inappropriate uses and artificial demand; recover compression heat; use no-loss auto drain traps; size piping for low pressure drop; maintain intercoolers and filters.
explain: This list is asked as a 5-mark short question almost every year. Back each item with a reason, for example '1 bar lower pressure saves about 6–10%' or 'every 4°C cooler intake saves about 1%'.
source: BEE 2024 P3 S2 / BEE 2025 P3 S-3

front: In a pump-up test, the receiver plus piping volume is 8.4 m³. With the compressor running and all users isolated, pressure rises from 2.0 to 8.0 bar(g) in 3.5 minutes. Atmospheric pressure is 1.013 bar(a). Estimate the FAD. If rated capacity is 16 m³/min, what is the capacity shortfall?
back: FAD ≈ 14.2 Nm³/min; shortfall ≈ 11% below rated.
explain: The pump-up test treats compression into the receiver as isothermal: free air delivered = (P2 − P1)/P0 × V ÷ T. If the compressed-air temperature differs from ambient, multiply by (273 + t_ambient)/(273 + t_air). A large shortfall points to worn valves or rings or a fouled intake filter.

front: How much cooling is 1 ton of refrigeration (TR)?
explain: It is the heat needed to melt 1 short ton of ice in 24 hours. Example: 27,216 kcal/h ÷ 3024 = 9 TR. In chilled-water systems, TR = flow (kg/h) × ΔT (°C) ÷ 3024.

front: How are COP and kW/TR related?
back: COP = cooling output ÷ power input (same units); kW/TR = 3.517 ÷ COP.
explain: For example, a chiller providing 100 kW of cooling at COP 4 draws 25 kW. COP 5.86 ≈ 0.6 kW/TR. A lower kW/TR is better. Energy Efficiency Ratio (EER) is often quoted interchangeably with COP in Indian practice (both are dimensionless ratios, though EER can also be in Btu/Wh).

front: What happens to the refrigerant in each component of a vapour compression cycle?
back: Evaporator: absorbs heat; liquid evaporates at low pressure. Compressor: raises pressure and temperature. Condenser: rejects heat; vapour condenses to liquid. Expansion valve: throttles, dropping pressure and temperature at constant enthalpy.
explain: Enthalpy changes across the compressor, condenser and evaporator, but expansion is (ideally) isenthalpic. In an ideal system the refrigerant temperature increases only in the compressor. Total heat rejected in the condenser = refrigeration effect + compressor work.

front: In a LiBr–water vapour absorption machine (VAM), which fluid is the refrigerant and which is the absorbent?
back: Water is the refrigerant; lithium bromide is the absorbent.
explain: Ammonia–water VAMs use ammonia as refrigerant and water as absorbent. Ammonia is the refrigerant common to both vapour compression and absorption systems. VAMs are driven by heat (steam, hot water, exhaust) with only small pump power, which makes them attractive where waste heat is available.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q47 / BEE 2025 P3 Q8

front: What is the effect of raising the chilled water leaving temperature (or evaporator temperature)?
back: It raises chiller efficiency (higher COP, lower kW/TR). About 3% compressor power is saved per 1°C rise in evaporator temperature.
explain: A higher evaporator temperature means higher suction pressure and a lower compression ratio, so less work per TR. Set the chilled water no colder than the process or comfort load needs. Likewise, a lower condensing temperature (cooler, clean condenser water) improves COP.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q48 / BEE 2025 P3 Q33

front: How does scale or fouling in condenser tubes affect a chiller?
back: It reduces heat transfer, raises condensing temperature and pressure, and increases compressor energy use.
explain: Fouling adds thermal resistance, so the refrigerant must condense at a higher temperature to reject the same heat. Watch the condenser approach (refrigerant condensing temperature − leaving water temperature). Tube cleaning and good cooling-water treatment restore performance.

front: Which rejects more heat per TR to the cooling tower: a vapour compression chiller or a VAM?
back: A VAM rejects much more, typically about 1.6–2 times as much, because it rejects both the refrigeration load and the driving heat input (low COP of about 0.7–1.3).
explain: Vapour compression chiller: heat rejected = 3024 + kW/TR × 860 kcal/h per TR (e.g. 0.6 kW/TR gives 3540 kcal/h per TR). VAM: 3024 + 3024/COP. So VAMs need larger cooling towers and more pumping. That must enter any economic comparison along with the cost of steam versus power.
source: BEE 2025 P3 S-6 / BEE 2024 P3 L5

front: If the dew point temperature equals the dry bulb temperature, what is the relative humidity?
back: 100%: the air is saturated.
explain: At saturation, dry bulb = wet bulb = dew point. The wider the gap between dry bulb and wet bulb, the drier the air and the greater the potential for evaporative cooling.

front: During evaporative cooling (air washer), what happens to dry bulb temperature, humidity ratio and enthalpy?
back: Dry bulb falls, humidity ratio rises, and enthalpy stays about constant (it follows the wet bulb line).
explain: Sensible heat in the air is converted to latent heat of the evaporated water, so total heat is essentially unchanged. Evaporative cooling works best in hot, dry climates.

front: What does an air-side economiser do in an HVAC system?
back: It uses cool outdoor air for 'free cooling' when outdoor conditions are favourable, reducing mechanical refrigeration.
explain: Dampers increase outdoor air intake when its enthalpy or temperature is below that of return air. Water-side economisers similarly use cooling-tower water to pre-cool chilled water in cold weather.

front: A chiller cools 100 m³/h of water from 12°C to 7°C. Compressor input is 150 kW. Find the cooling load in TR, kW/TR and COP. If the condenser water ΔT is 5°C, what condenser water flow is needed?
back: ≈ 165.3 TR; 0.907 kW/TR; COP ≈ 3.88; condenser water ≈ 125.8 m³/h.
explain: Chilled-water TR uses m·cp·ΔT. The condenser must reject the refrigeration effect plus the compressor work (kW × 860 kcal/kWh), which is why condenser flow exceeds chilled water flow at the same ΔT. These are the standard steps of a chiller performance assessment.

steps.explain: Q = m·cp·ΔT, with cp of water = 1 kcal/kg°C.
1 TR = 3024 kcal/h.
Specific power consumption.
COP = cooling kW / input kW = 3.517/(kW/TR).

steps.explain: Heat rejected = cooling + work.

front: What is the Energy Performance Index (EPI) of a building, and what is its unit?
back: EPI = total annual energy consumption ÷ built-up area, in kWh/m²/year.
explain: BEE star ratings for buildings use EPI bands; a lower EPI earns more stars. Use the built-up area (not carpet area) unless the rating scheme specifies otherwise. Total consumption includes grid plus DG/captive electricity.

front: Which buildings does the ECBC / Energy Conservation Act provision on buildings apply to?
back: Commercial buildings with a connected load of 100 kW or more (or contract demand of 120 kVA or more).
explain: ECBC compliance can be shown by the prescriptive approach, the trade-off approach (Envelope Performance Factor, EPF), or the whole-building performance approach using simulation. EPF compares the envelope of the proposed design against a baseline.

front: What does the Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (SHGC) of a window measure?
back: The fraction of incident solar radiation admitted through the fenestration as heat. For SHGC 0.25 and 600 W/m² incident, gain = 150 W/m².
explain: A lower SHGC means less solar heat gain and lower cooling load. Visible Light Transmittance (VLT) measures daylight separately. Effective Aperture = VLT × Window-to-Wall Ratio. ECBC defines a skylight as fenestration sloped less than 60° from horizontal.

front: What is the difference between U-value, thermal emittance and solar reflectance (cool roof)?
back: U-value = overall heat transfer coefficient through an assembly (W/m²K); lower means better insulation. Thermal emittance = a surface's ability to re-radiate absorbed heat. Solar reflectance = the fraction of sunlight reflected; high reflectance makes a cool roof.
explain: Emissivity is the ratio of energy radiated by a material to that of a black body at the same temperature. Thermal bridging is a conductive path (e.g. through steel or concrete frames) that bypasses insulation. Thermal mass stores heat in building materials and delays peak loads.
source: BEE 2025 P3 S-4 / BEE 2024 P3 S5

front: State the fan (and pump) affinity laws for a change in speed.
back: Flow ∝ N; pressure (head) ∝ N²; power ∝ N³.
explain: The same laws apply to speed changes made by VFD, pulley change or two-speed motors, and they assume the system curve passes through the origin (no static head). For fans the power also scales with air density. The cube law is why speed control saves so much more energy than damper throttling.

front: By how much does fan power fall if the speed is reduced by 10%?
back: About 27%, since 0.9³ = 0.729.
explain: Similarly, 16 kW at 800 rpm falls to 16 × (600/800)³ = 6.75 kW at 600 rpm. Reducing a fan from 49 Hz to 34 Hz cuts power by about 1 − (34/49)³ ≈ 67%. A 52 kW fan would then save about 34.6 kW.

front: What happens to fan airflow when system resistance increases (e.g. clogged filter, closed damper)?
back: Airflow decreases: the operating point moves left along the fan curve to a higher pressure and lower flow.
explain: The operating point is where the fan curve meets the system resistance curve (ΔP ∝ Q²). Larger ducts, smooth bends and clean filters reduce resistance. Dampers and filter fouling change the system curve; speed changes and inlet guide vanes change the fan curve.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q1 / BEE 2025 P3 Q27

front: Rank the common fan flow control methods by energy efficiency.
back: Best to worst: speed control (VFD or variable speed coupling), then inlet guide vanes, then outlet damper throttling.
explain: Throttling with a damper wastes energy across the damper while the fan stays at full speed. Inlet guide vanes pre-swirl the air and give moderate savings. VFDs follow the cube law, so they give the largest savings when flow is reduced substantially. Pulley changes suit permanent flow reductions.

front: How is fan static efficiency calculated from field measurements?
back: η_static = (Q × ΔP_static) / (102 × shaft power), with Q in m³/s, ΔP in mmWC and power in kW.
explain: Q is found by pitot traverse: velocity v = Cp × √(2g × Δp_velocity(mmWC) / ρ) m/s, then Q = v × duct area. Shaft power = motor input × motor efficiency (× gearbox or belt efficiency, if present). The constant 102 converts mmWC·m³/s to kW.

front: A centrifugal fan runs at 1480 rpm, delivering 36,000 m³/h at 350 mmWC and drawing 45 kW. Its speed is reduced to 1180 rpm with a VFD. Find the new flow, pressure, power and power saving (ignore VFD losses).
back: Flow ≈ 28,700 m³/h; pressure ≈ 222 mmWC; power ≈ 22.8 kW; saving ≈ 22.2 kW.
explain: The affinity laws give flow ∝ N, pressure ∝ N² and power ∝ N³. A 20% speed reduction halves the power. In real systems with significant static pressure, savings are somewhat lower than the pure cube law predicts.

steps.explain: Q ∝ N.
P ∝ N².
kW ∝ N³.
Difference in input power.

front: What is the formula for the hydraulic (water) power of a pump?
back: P_hydraulic (kW) = Q (m³/s) × H (m) × ρ (kg/m³) × g / 1000. Pump efficiency = hydraulic power ÷ shaft power.
explain: Example: 200 m³/h at 30 m gives (200/3600) × 30 × 1000 × 9.81 / 1000 = 16.35 kW of hydraulic power. At 70% efficiency, input = 23.36 kW. Shaft power = motor input × motor efficiency.

front: If pump speed is reduced to two-thirds, what happens to power?
back: Power falls to (2/3)³ ≈ 0.30, about 30% of the original, while flow falls to 67% and head to 44%.
explain: This assumes a purely frictional system. Where a large static head exists, the pump may deliver much less flow (or none) at reduced speed, so check the system curve before relying on the cube law.

front: Why is a centrifugal pump impeller trimmed, and what happens to flow, head and power?
back: To permanently reduce capacity to match the real system requirement (instead of throttling). Flow ∝ D, head ∝ D², power ∝ D³, so trimming reduces head.
explain: Example: a 230 mm impeller delivering 150 m³/h, trimmed for 110 m³/h, becomes about 230 × 110/150 ≈ 169 mm. Trimming is irreversible and works best for small reductions (generally within about 10–20%). A VFD is preferred where demand varies.

front: What is cavitation in a pump, and how is NPSH related to it?
back: Cavitation is the formation and violent collapse of vapour bubbles when local pressure falls below vapour pressure. It erodes the impeller, causes noise and vibration, and reduces head. It is avoided when NPSH available exceeds NPSH required.
explain: NPSHA rises with a higher suction-side liquid level, larger suction pipe diameter (less friction), shorter suction lines and cooler liquid. Increasing the suction pipe diameter therefore increases NPSHA. NPSHR is a property of the pump and rises with flow.

front: A pump designed for 40 lps at 20 m is operating at 16 m head. What happens to flow, efficiency and power?
back: Flow rises above rated, efficiency falls (the pump has moved right of its BEP), and power drawn rises above rated.
explain: On a centrifugal pump curve, lower head means higher flow. Moving away from the best efficiency point (BEP) on either side lowers efficiency. For most centrifugal pumps, power rises with flow, so the motor may also be overloaded.

front: What is the efficiency of a centrifugal pump at shut-off head (zero flow)?
back: 0%: no useful hydraulic work is done, because Q = 0.
explain: At shut-off, all the input power becomes heat in the liquid, which can overheat the pump. That is why minimum-flow recirculation lines are provided. Efficiency peaks at the BEP and falls to zero at both shut-off and run-out.

front: What are common symptoms of an oversized pump, and what is the best fix?
back: A heavily throttled discharge valve, high pressure drop across the valve, high noise or vibration, and frequent bypass or recirculation. Fix it by trimming the impeller, fitting a smaller pump or impeller, or using a VFD, not by replacing only the motor or fitting a larger impeller.
explain: Throttling wastes the excess head across the valve. If a pump runs at about 30% of rated flow, a correctly sized pump (or speed reduction) gives the largest saving. Larger diameter pipes also reduce friction head and system resistance.

front: Why do VFD savings on pumps depend on the ratio of static head to friction head?
back: Speed reduction must still overcome the fixed static head, so the cube-law saving is only achieved in friction-dominated systems. In static-head-dominated systems, savings are much smaller and efficiency drops.
explain: The system curve is H = H_static + k·Q². When H_static is large, a small speed reduction moves the operating point far down the flow axis and away from the BEP. Always plot the pump curves at reduced speed against the actual system curve.

front: A cooling water pump delivers 180 m³/h. Discharge pressure is 3.2 kg/cm² (about 32 m) and the suction lift is 3 m. The motor draws 28 kW at 90% efficiency. Find the pump efficiency. If the impeller (250 mm) is trimmed so the pump delivers 150 m³/h, estimate the new diameter and shaft power.
back: Pump efficiency ≈ 68%; trimmed impeller ≈ 208 mm; new shaft power ≈ 14.6 kW.
explain: Total head = discharge head + suction lift (if the source is below the pump), or discharge − suction head (if the source is above, i.e. flooded suction). Hydraulic power is ρgQH, and shaft power is motor input × motor efficiency. The impeller trim estimate uses the diameter affinity laws.

steps.explain: With a suction lift, add it to the discharge head.
P = Q·H·ρ·g/1000 with ρ = 1000.
Motor output = input × η_motor.
η_pump = hydraulic / shaft power.

steps.prompt: Find the trimmed diameter and new power.
steps.explain: Q ∝ D, P ∝ D³.

front: Define cooling tower range, approach and effectiveness.
back: Range = hot water in − cold water out. Approach = cold water out − ambient wet bulb temperature. Effectiveness = range ÷ (range + approach).
explain: Example: inlet 40°C, range 10°C, approach 5°C gives outlet 30°C and wet bulb 25°C. Approach (not the dry bulb) is the better indicator of tower performance; the lower the approach, the better. The wet bulb temperature is the theoretical lower limit for the cold water.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q9 / BEE 2025 P3 L-1

front: What is the formula for cooling tower evaporation loss?
back: Evaporation (m³/h) ≈ 0.00085 × 1.8 × circulation rate (m³/h) × range (°C).
explain: Roughly 1% of circulating water is evaporated for every 7°C (about 5.5°C in some texts) of range. Evaporation is the useful cooling mechanism; drift (water carried out as droplets) and blowdown are the other losses.

front: How are blowdown and make-up related to Cycles of Concentration (COC)?
back: Blowdown = Evaporation ÷ (COC − 1). Make-up = Evaporation + Drift + Blowdown. For example, 12 m³/h evaporation at COC 2.5 needs 8 m³/h blowdown.
explain: COC = dissolved solids in circulating water ÷ dissolved solids in make-up water, i.e. how many times water is reused before discharge. Raising COC (with better treatment) cuts blowdown and make-up, but risks scaling, corrosion and fouling.

front: What is the most influential component of a cooling tower, and what does it do?
back: The fill media: it increases water–air contact area and contact time for heat and mass transfer.
explain: Splash fills break water into droplets. Film fills spread water into thin films and are more efficient, but they clog more easily with poor water quality. Clogged or damaged fill raises the approach directly.

front: If three of the four parameters (heat load, range, approach, wet bulb) are held constant, how does the required cooling tower size vary with the fourth?
back: Directly with heat load; inversely with range; inversely with approach; inversely with wet bulb temperature.
explain: A smaller approach demands a disproportionately larger tower. A higher range for the same approach and wet bulb means hotter inlet water and a bigger driving force, so a smaller tower suffices. A lower design wet bulb requires a larger tower.

front: List energy-saving measures for cooling towers.
back: Clean and maintain fill and nozzles; use FRP blades and set the blade angle seasonally; fit VFDs or two-speed fans controlled on cold water temperature; maintain correct water chemistry and COC; balance flow across cells; avoid air recirculation and bypass.
explain: Better tower performance lowers cold water temperature, which in turn cuts chiller or condenser energy. That system effect is often larger than the fan saving itself.
source: BEE 2025 P3 Q31 / BEE 2024 P3 Q10

front: A cooling tower circulates 1500 m³/h. Hot water is at 40°C, cold water at 32°C, and the ambient wet bulb is 28°C. Find the range, approach, effectiveness, heat rejected (TR), evaporation loss and blowdown at COC 4 (neglect drift).
back: Range 8°C; approach 4°C; effectiveness 66.7%; ≈ 3968 TR; evaporation ≈ 18.4 m³/h; blowdown ≈ 6.1 m³/h; make-up ≈ 24.5 m³/h.
explain: This combines every standard cooling-tower formula in one question. Evaporation uses the 0.00085 × 1.8 × flow × range rule, and blowdown follows from E/(COC − 1). Make-up replaces evaporation + blowdown (+ drift).

steps.explain: Definitions.
Range/(range + approach).
Q = m·cp·ΔT.
BEE empirical formula.
Blowdown = E/(COC − 1).

source: BEE 2025 P3 L-1 / BEE 2024 P3 S7 (similar)

front: What is luminous efficacy, and what is its unit?
back: The ratio of light output to electrical input, in lumens per watt (lm/W).
explain: It is not the same as luminance (brightness of a surface, cd/m²) or illuminance (lux = lm/m²). Comparing efficacy, including control gear losses, is the basis for choosing an efficient lamp. LEDs offer high efficacy along with good colour rendering.

front: Is the lumen weighted most heavily towards blue light?
back: No. The lumen is weighted by the eye's photopic sensitivity curve, which peaks in the green-yellow (about 555 nm), not blue.
explain: That is why low-pressure sodium (monochromatic yellow) lamps have very high efficacy but render colour very poorly. The CRI scale runs to 100, where colours look identical to a reference source. Colour-critical tasks need lamps with high CRI.
source: BEE 2024 P3 L1 / BEE 2025 P3 Q9

front: What is the function of a luminaire?
back: To distribute, control and direct the light from the lamp (plus housing, protecting and connecting it). It does not generate light itself.
explain: Efficient luminaires with good optics and reflectors put more lumens on the working plane. That raises the utilisation factor and allows fewer lamps for the same illuminance.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q11 / BEE 2025 P3 Q34

front: What is Lighting Power Density (LPD), and how is the lighting power allowance calculated?
back: LPD = installed lighting watts ÷ floor area (W/m²). Allowance = LPD limit × floor area. For example, 14 floors × 1000 m² × 10.8 W/m² = 1,51,200 W.
explain: ECBC sets maximum LPD values by building type (building area method) or by space (space function method). Lower installed LPD for the same lux means a more efficient design.

front: What is ILER, and how is it interpreted?
back: Installed Load Efficacy Ratio = actual installed load efficacy (lux/W/m²) ÷ target efficacy for that application. ILER of 0.75 or above is satisfactory; 0.51–0.74 needs review; 0.5 or below needs urgent action.
explain: Installed load efficacy = average maintained lux ÷ (installed W/m²). It is a quick audit indicator of how well the lighting system converts power into useful illuminance.

front: A 20 m × 15 m workshop needs 400 lux. Luminaires are 36 W LED, each producing 4000 lumens. Utilisation factor is 0.65 and maintenance factor is 0.8. Find the number of luminaires, the installed LPD, and the installed load efficacy (lux/W/m²).
back: 58 luminaires; LPD ≈ 6.96 W/m²; installed load efficacy ≈ 57.5 lux/W/m².
explain: The lumen method divides the total lumens needed on the working plane by the effective lumens per luminaire after UF and MF. The LPD check is what ECBC compliance looks at. Installed load efficacy compared with the target gives the ILER.

steps.prompt: Find the area and total lumens required.
steps.explain: Φ = E × A.

steps.prompt: Find the effective lumens per luminaire.
steps.explain: Lamp lumens × UF × MF.
Always round up.

steps.prompt: Find the installed load and LPD.
steps.explain: LPD = W/m².
Lux ÷ W/m².

front: How is hourly fuel consumption of a DG set found from kVA, PF and specific fuel consumption?
back: Fuel (L/h) = kVA × PF × SFC (L/kWh). For example, 1250 kVA × 0.8 × 0.23 = 230 L/h; 1000 kVA × 0.7 × 0.25 = 175 L/h.
explain: kVA × PF gives kW, and kW × 1 h × L/kWh gives litres. The inverse, kWh per litre (specific energy generation), is the usual DG performance indicator. Typical well-loaded DG sets achieve about 3–4 kWh/L.
source: BEE 2024 P3 Q18 / BEE 2025 P3 Q46

front: In a DG set, which loss is the largest?
back: Flue (exhaust) gas loss, followed by cooling water (jacket) loss.
explain: Only about 30–40% of fuel energy becomes electricity. The hot exhaust (typically 400–500°C) can drive a waste heat boiler or VAM, especially when the DG runs continuously. Stack exit temperature is kept above the acid dew point.
source: BEE 2025 P3 Q5 / BEE 2024 P3 S1

front: How do altitude and high ambient temperature affect a DG set?
back: They reduce power output (the set must be derated), because thinner, hotter air holds less oxygen mass for combustion.
explain: Manufacturers give derating factors for altitude, ambient temperature and humidity. Choose the DG capacity using site-derated output, not nameplate rating.

front: Name good operating practices for DG set energy efficiency.
back: Load the set near its optimum (typically above about 60–70%); avoid low-load running; operate parallel sets to share load sensibly; keep phase loads balanced; maintain PF near the rated 0.8 or above; keep intake air cool and clean; recover exhaust heat; monitor kWh per litre.
explain: Alternator losses rise at low PF because higher current is drawn for the same kW, so alternator losses are not independent of PF. DG sets are not designed to tolerate large phase unbalance (such as 25%); unbalance causes alternator overheating.

front: A 500 kVA DG set (rated PF 0.8) supplies an average of 320 kW for 1 hour on test and consumes 95 litres of diesel (density 0.85 kg/L, GCV 10,800 kcal/kg). Find the percentage loading, specific energy generation (kWh/L), overall thermal efficiency, and the fuel cost per kWh at Rs 90/L.
back: Loading 80%; ≈ 3.37 kWh/L; efficiency ≈ 31.6%; ≈ Rs 26.7/kWh.
explain: DG performance is tracked by kWh per litre (or its inverse, SFC in L/kWh). Overall efficiency = electrical output (kWh × 860 kcal/kWh) ÷ fuel heat input. A falling kWh/L trend signals poor loading, injector or turbocharger problems.

steps.explain: Loading on kW rating.
kWh per litre.
Mass × GCV.
1 kWh = 860 kcal.

steps.prompt: Find the fuel cost per kWh.
steps.explain: Fuel price ÷ kWh/L.

front: Why does a VFD save the most energy on centrifugal pumps and fans?
back: These are variable-torque loads whose power varies with speed³. Matching speed to demand, instead of throttling, captures cube-law savings.
explain: Constant-torque loads (conveyors, positive-displacement pumps, screw compressors) save roughly in proportion to speed, so savings are smaller but still worthwhile where output varies. VFDs also give soft starting. The trade-offs are VFD losses (about 2–4%) and harmonic generation.

front: Name the five components of an electric power supply system.
back: Generating units, high-voltage transmission lines, distribution lines, substations, and energy control centres.
explain: Generators produce electricity, transmission lines carry it over long distances, distribution lines deliver it to consumers, and substations connect the pieces. Energy control centres coordinate the operation of all components.

front: What is the heat rate of a power plant, and in what units is it expressed?
back: The heat input (in kcal or kJ) needed to generate one kWh of electrical output.
explain: One kWh is equivalent to 860 kcal or 3600 kJ of thermal energy. Heat rate is inversely proportional to efficiency, so a coal plant at 28-35% efficiency has a heat rate of roughly 2450-3070 kcal/kWh.

front: What are the sub-transmission and distribution voltage levels named in this chapter?
back: Sub-transmission: 132, 110, 66 or 33 kV. Distribution (last link to the consumer): 11, 6.6 or 3.3 kV.
explain: Sub-stations containing step-down transformers reduce the voltage at each link. Consumers connect directly at distribution voltage or through transformers, depending on the level of service.

front: If the distribution voltage is raised from 11 kV to 33 kV for the same power and the same line, by what factor does the line power loss fall?
back: To 1/9 of the original (nine times lower).
explain: Current falls in proportion to voltage for the same power, and line loss depends on the current squared, so the voltage ratio enters the loss calculation squared.

steps.explain: The ratio sets how much the current and voltage drop change.

steps.prompt: How does the current change for the same power?
steps.answer: Current is inversely proportional to voltage, so it falls to 1/3.
steps.explain: For a fixed power, current is proportional to 1/V.

steps.prompt: How does the voltage drop change?
steps.answer: Voltage drop falls by a factor of 1/3.
steps.explain: Drop is proportional to the line current for the same resistance and length.

steps.prompt: How does the line loss change?
steps.answer: Loss is proportional to I2R, so the factor is (1/3)2 = 1/9 of the original.
steps.explain: Squaring the current reduction gives the nine-fold saving.

front: Why must electricity be generated only as and when it is needed?
back: Electricity cannot be stored in the system in bulk, so generation must match demand at every instant.
explain: This is why load management matters: peaks force utilities to add or run costly capacity, so reducing peak demand benefits both the utility and the consumer.

front: What is the standard technical T&D loss in India, and why do state figures run higher?
back: Standard technical losses are about 17% (efficiency 83%). State T&D losses range from 17% to 50% because unmetered supply and pilferage are also counted.
explain: Only part of the gap is technical; the rest is commercial loss from theft, unmetered use and billing failures. The 83% efficiency is the benchmark against which state figures are compared.

front: Find the overall T&D cascade efficiency from plant output to end use, using stage efficiencies of 99.5%, 99%, 97.5%, 96%, 99.5% and 95%.
explain: Energy passes through each stage in turn, so the stage efficiencies multiply to give the cascade efficiency from generation to the user.

steps.prompt: Multiply the step-up and EHV stage efficiencies.
steps.explain: Step-up station and EHV transmission are the first two stages.

steps.prompt: Multiply by the HV transmission stage.
steps.explain: Each stage multiplies the energy that passes on to the next.
Sub-transmission at 66/132 kV is the fourth stage.

steps.prompt: Multiply by the distribution step-down stage.
steps.explain: Step-down to 11/33 kV is the fifth stage.

steps.prompt: Multiply by the primary distribution stage and express as a percentage.
steps.explain: This matches the chapter's cascade efficiency result.

front: Plant-level stage efficiencies are: T&D 83%, in-plant distribution including transformer 95%, motor 90% and mechanical (drive, pump, valve) 70%. What is the overall end-use efficiency, and how many units must be generated to deliver one unit saved at the end use?
back: About 50%. One unit saved at the end user equals two units generated (1 / 0.5).
explain: Savings at the point of use are multiplied back through the whole chain, which is why end-use savings are so valuable.

steps.prompt: Multiply the T&D and in-plant distribution efficiencies.
steps.explain: Power from the grid passes through the T&D network and the plant distribution system.
Motor efficiency is the next link in the chain.
Coupling, drive train, pump and throttling losses make up the last stage.

steps.prompt: Find the units generated per unit saved at the end use.
steps.explain: The chapter's rule: one unit saved at the end user equals two units generated at the plant.

front: In one 30-minute recording interval a load draws 2500 kVA for 4 min, 3600 kVA for 12 min, 4100 kVA for 6 min and 3800 kVA for 8 min. What maximum demand does the meter record?
back: About 3606.7 kVA (the time-integrated average over the 30-minute interval).
explain: The meter records the average demand over the interval, not the instantaneous peak. The 4100 kVA peak lasts only 6 minutes and is averaged down.

steps.prompt: Compute the kVA-minutes for each segment.
steps.explain: Demand multiplied by time gives the energy drawn in that segment.
This is the total energy over the interval.

steps.prompt: Check that the durations add up to the recording interval.
steps.explain: Confirms no time is missed or double counted.
The interval average is the maximum demand recorded for that cycle.

front: What minimum quantities does a utility's trivector meter record for billing?
back: Maximum demand (kVA) in the month, active energy (kWh), reactive energy (kVArh) and apparent energy (kVAh) for the billing cycle.
explain: Maximum demand is measured over preset intervals (e.g. 30 minutes) and reset at the end of every billing cycle. The highest interval value is billed even if it lasts only one interval.

front: On what basis may a utility bill maximum demand when it uses minimum billing demand?
back: On the higher of actual recorded demand and a minimum of 75% to 100% of contract demand.
explain: Under this clause a plant can pay for demand it did not draw. Compare contract demand with recorded demand before deciding whether to surrender any of it.

front: Define power factor in terms of kW and kVA.
back: PF = kW / kVA = cos phi. It is always less than or equal to 1.
explain: kW is the active power doing work, kVAr is the reactive power that builds magnetic fields, and kVA is their vector sum, which is the load the distribution system actually carries. Inductive industrial loads often run at PF 0.2 to 0.9.

front: Name four benefits of improving power factor by adding capacitors.
back: Lower total current and reactive component from the source; lower I2R losses; higher voltage at the load end; kVA loading relief on generators, transformers and lines.
explain: The freed capacity lets the same transformer or feeder carry more load. Lower kVA also reduces maximum demand charges and avoids PF penalties.

front: A 1500 kVA transformer supplies a plant drawing 1160 kVA at PF 0.70. If 410 kVAr of capacitors is added, what are the new kVA, PF and transformer loading?
back: About 913 kVA, PF 0.89, and about 60% loading (913 / 1500).
explain: Capacitors cut the reactive part of the load, so kVA falls while kW stays the same.

steps.explain: kW = kVA x PF. Adding capacitors does not change kW.
kVA^2 = kW^2 + kVAr^2.
Capacitors supply part of the reactive power locally.
The reduced kVA is the new load on the transformer.

steps.prompt: Find the new PF and transformer loading.
steps.explain: The transformer gains spare capacity for future loads.

front: Why are automatic power factor controllers used where loads fluctuate, instead of fixed capacitor banks?
back: Fixed banks cannot hold PF near unity when the load fluctuates. At light load the PF can go leading, raising motor-terminal voltage and maximum demand, so the controller switches banks on and off to track the set PF.
explain: The controller displays PF at the point of supply, compares it with the target, and switches capacitor steps through relay outputs. Typically 6 to 14 relays are provided.

front: A plant's average load is 627 kW at PF 0.72. How many kVAr of capacitors are needed to raise the PF to 0.95?
back: About 398 kVAr (install a 400 kVAr bank).
explain: kVAr = kW x (tan phi1 - tan phi2). The chapter's multiplier table gives the same answer (0.635 for 0.72 to 0.95).

steps.answer: cos phi1 = 0.72, so tan phi1 = 0.964 (chapter value).
steps.explain: Use the inverse cosine to get the angle, then its tangent.
Same method for the target power factor.

steps.prompt: Find the difference of the tangents.
steps.explain: This is the multiplier per kW of load.
This is the reactive power the capacitors must supply.
Round up to the nearest available capacitor rating.

front: Where should power factor capacitors be placed to give the maximum benefit?
back: As close as possible to the load, ideally at each piece of equipment, so that the kVAr is confined to the smallest possible segment and current and losses fall.
explain: Losses are proportional to the square of the current, so capacitors near the load cut losses across the system. Motor voltage and performance also improve.

front: What is the largest capacitor rating that should be connected at a motor's terminals?
back: Not greater than the motor's no-load magnetising kVAr. Larger units can cause damaging over-voltage or transient torques.
explain: Motor makers usually specify maximum capacitor ratings for each motor. Individual motor correction is generally economic from about 10 HP upward.

front: What is the energy-efficiency limitation of placing PF capacitors only at the main service or receiving substation?
back: It reduces losses only on the utility side. It does not reduce losses inside the plant network and does not improve the load capability of the distribution system.
explain: Tail-end correction in the plant's own network also cuts losses there and directly reduces consumption. Main-service capacitors are cheapest to install but usually need switching to control the capacitance.

front: Are single-phase motor-starting capacitors or lighting voltage-boost capacitors suitable for power factor correction?
back: No. They are not power factor capacitor units and cannot withstand power-system conditions.
explain: Check PF capacitors by their charging current, since nameplates can mislead and some capacitor boxes contain no capacitor elements.

front: How is the secondary voltage of a transformer related to its turns ratio?
back: Secondary voltage = primary voltage x turns ratio (secondary turns / primary turns). Primary ampere-turns equal secondary ampere-turns.
explain: Stepping voltage up lowers the current for the same power, which is why power is generated at low voltage, transmitted at high voltage and suffers less line loss.

front: How are transformers classified by voltage in this chapter?
back: Power transformers for transmission (400, 220, 110, 66 and 33 kV). Distribution transformers for distribution networks (11, 6.6, 3.3 kV, 440 V and 230 V).
explain: The OCR text reads 200 kV for the transmission level; 220 kV is used here, matching the chapter's transmission voltages. Distribution transformers connect the network to end users.

front: What is diversity factor, and what is its range?
back: Diversity factor = overall maximum demand of the plant / sum of the individual maximum demands of its loads. It is always less than one.
explain: Transformer kVA rating = connected load x diversity factor for the industry. The factor depends on individual loads, load factor and future expansion plans.

front: What must two transformers have in common before they are operated in parallel?
back: Same phase-angle displacement, same voltage ratio, same percentage impedance, same polarity and same phase sequence.
explain: Technically identical units with matching impedance minimise circulating current. Parallel operation also lets the load be shared as it fluctuates, keeping transformers near their maximum efficiency range.

front: From what date are distribution transformers under the BEE Standards & Labelling programme, and what does 1 star represent?
back: Mandatory from 7 January 2010. 1 star is the base case, equal to the IS 1180 (Part 1) loss levels; 5 star is the lowest-loss segment.
explain: Labelling is based on total losses at 50% and 100% loading. A higher star rating means lower losses.

front: List four factors that increase technical losses in a distribution system.
back: Lengthy radial LT and 11 kV lines in rural areas; undersized conductors for load growth; distribution transformers not located at the load centre; low power factor.
explain: Each raises I2R loss: long lines add resistance, undersized conductors run hot, distant transformers force long secondary runs with voltage drop, and low PF draws more current.

front: What are the normative total technical loss limits in Indian transmission and distribution networks?
back: Total 7.0% minimum to 15.5% maximum. Components: step-up and EHV 0.5-1.0%; transmission to intermediate voltage and step-down to sub-transmission 1.5-3.0%; sub-transmission to distribution 2.0-4.5%; distribution lines and service connections 3.0-7.0%.
explain: The component minimums add up to 7.0 and the maximums add up to 15.5, which gives the total range in the chapter's Table 1.6.

back: About 13.4 kW, roughly half the original (ratio 0.49).
explain: At the same kW, a lower PF means higher kVA and current. Loss depends on current squared, so loss scales with (PF before / PF after) squared.

front: What is collection efficiency, and how does it feed into AT&C loss?
back: Collection efficiency = amount collected / total amount billed x 100%. AT&C loss = [1 - (billing efficiency x collection efficiency)] x 100.
explain: AT&C combines technical losses (captured by billing efficiency) and commercial losses such as theft, meter tampering and poor collection into one utility-level figure.

front: What is Demand Side Management (DSM)?
back: Actions taken on the customer's side of the meter to change the amount (kWh) or timing (kVA) of energy consumption, so as to avoid or postpone building new generating plants.
explain: DSM aims to maximise end-use efficiency. It is often more cost-effective and resource-efficient than adding supply capacity.

front: List the five steps of the DSM implementation methodology.
back: 1. Load research; 2. Define load-shape objectives; 3. Assess programme implementation strategies; 4. Implementation; 5. Monitoring and evaluation.
explain: Load research profiles the customer base, tariff and hourly load to find the peak-load contributors. Evaluation compares results with the utility's goal using a benefit-cost analysis.

front: What are the two broad types of DSM measures?
back: (a) Energy reduction programmes, which cut demand through more efficient processes, buildings or equipment. (b) Load management programmes, which shift load away from peak times and peak rates.
explain: Examples of (a): efficient lighting, efficient motors, preventive maintenance and energy audit. Examples of (b): load levelling, time-of-use tariffs and power-factor penalties.

front: Define peak clipping and valley filling as load-shape objectives.
back: Peak clipping: reducing utility load mainly during peak-demand periods. Valley filling: building load in off-peak periods to improve the system load factor.
explain: Load shifting combines the two, reducing peak load while building off-peak load, and typically leaves total electricity sales largely unchanged. Conservation, by contrast, reduces load across most hours.

front: What is a harmonic, and what frequency is the 5th harmonic on a 50 Hz system?
back: A harmonic is a component frequency that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency. The 5th harmonic on a 50 Hz system is 250 Hz.
explain: Harmonics come from non-linear loads. Harmonic current cannot be used by equipment on the network, so it is converted to heat and wasted, and it can travel back into the supply.

explain: Current THD is the root-sum-square of the harmonic currents divided by the fundamental. A simple linear sum would give 34%, so the RSS form is the one that matches the chapter's result.

steps.explain: Harmonic currents are combined on a root-sum-square basis.

front: What is the individual odd-harmonic current limit (h below 11) and the TDD limit for a system with Isc/IL below 20?
back: Individual limit 4.0% of IL for h below 11; total demand distortion (TDD) limit 5.0%.
explain: Even harmonics are limited to 25% of the odd-harmonic limits. Distortion that causes a DC offset, such as from half-wave converters, is not allowed. Limits apply at the point of common coupling.

front: What advantages does an active front-end (AFE) rectifier in a VFD offer for harmonics?
back: It mitigates harmonics without external filters, keeps unity power factor at the point of common coupling, allows energy to flow back to the mains, and holds the DC-link voltage steady despite supply variations.
explain: An LCL filter between the grid and the AFE bypasses the high-frequency switching harmonics, so the grid sees a near-sinusoidal supply.

front: Who is responsible for limiting current distortion, and who for voltage distortion?
back: The customer limits current distortion; the utility limits voltage distortion.
explain: Limits apply at the point of common coupling (PCC), usually the utility ownership or metering point, so the whole plant is judged there rather than individual panels or equipment.

front: Which tool is used to find loose or corroded connections and hot spots in distribution equipment?
back: An infra-red (IR) camera.
explain: Poor connections raise resistance, causing hot spots, voltage drops and energy waste. Such checks support reliability-centred maintenance, which the chapter notes can save money, energy and downtime.

front: What four operating components are common to all electric motors?
back: Stator (stationary windings), rotor (rotating windings), bearings and frame (enclosure).
explain: These four parts are present in induction, DC and synchronous motors alike. The motor types differ mainly in how the windings are energised and arranged.

front: Why does an induction motor rotor always run slower than the stator's rotating field?
back: Relative motion between the rotating flux and the rotor conductors is needed to induce rotor current. Lenz's law makes the rotor current oppose that relative motion, so the rotor chases the field but never catches it.
explain: The EMF induced in the rotor has the same frequency as the supply. If the rotor matched the field speed there would be no relative motion, no induced current and no torque.

front: How does a slip-ring (wound-rotor) motor differ from a squirrel cage motor?
back: Its rotor is wound with coils whose ends go to slip rings. Carbon brushes on the rings let external resistors or contactors be added in series with the rotor.
explain: Extra rotor resistance moves the pull-out torque to a lower speed, so the motor gives high torque at low starting current. The resistance is cut out once the motor reaches base speed, which suits very high inertia loads.

front: Down to what speed can rotor resistors slow a slip-ring motor at full load before efficiency falls sharply?
back: About 50% of synchronous speed. Below that, power dissipated in the rotor resistances makes efficiency very low.
explain: Slip-ring motors suit variable torque, variable speed loads such as printing presses, compressors, conveyor belts, hoists and elevators. Rotor-resistance speed control wastes energy as heat, so it is best kept above about 50% speed.

front: How is the rotor of a synchronous motor energised, and how does its speed compare with the supply?
back: A separate DC source feeds the rotor. It locks onto the stator's rotating field and runs at synchronous speed with no slip.
explain: Synchronous speed depends only on supply frequency and the number of poles. Because there is no slip, the DC excitation supplies the energy that slip would otherwise provide in an induction motor.

front: Which pole counts does the chapter list for motors on 50 Hz mains?
back: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 16 poles. The pole count is always even.
explain: Synchronous speed (rpm) = 120 × frequency (Hz) / number of poles, so a 4-pole motor on 50 Hz runs at 120 × 50 / 4 = 1500 rpm. The pole count is fixed at construction, so speed can only be changed by frequency (VFD) or a different winding.

front: How is motor slip (%) defined?
back: Slip (%) = (Synchronous speed − full-load rated speed) / Synchronous speed × 100.
explain: Slip is the speed gap that lets the rotor induce current and produce torque. The chapter notes that nameplate full-load slip is not accurate, so measuring slip under full load gives better results.

front: Why are induction motors the main reason for low power factor in electrical systems?
back: Induction motors are inductive loads with PF below one, and their power factor drops as the load falls. Motors running well below rated capacity therefore pull the plant PF down.
explain: As load comes down, the active current reduces and the motor PF reduces with it. Oversized or lightly loaded motors are the usual cause of this problem.

front: How is motor efficiency defined?
back: Mechanical energy delivered at the rotating shaft divided by the electrical energy input at the motor terminals.
explain: Because motor PF is below one, more current is needed for the same real power, and upstream wiring losses rise with the square of current. A high efficiency and a PF close to unity are both wanted for efficient plant operation.

front: Which motors are more efficient: squirrel cage or slip-ring, TEFC or SPDP, higher speed or lower speed, larger or smaller rating?
back: Squirrel cage beats slip-ring; higher-speed motors beat lower-speed ones; TEFC beats SPDP; and efficiency rises with rated capacity.
explain: Efficiency also depends on motor temperature. TEFC means totally enclosed, fan-cooled, and SPDP means screen-protected, drip-proof.

front: Which motor losses are fixed (load-independent) and which are variable (load-dependent)?
back: Fixed: magnetic core (iron) losses and friction and windage. Variable: stator and rotor resistance (I²R) losses and stray load losses.
explain: Core losses are eddy current and hysteresis losses in the stator steel. Stray losses vary roughly with the square of the rotor current and are hard to measure directly. Intrinsic losses can only be cut by changing the motor design.

front: What stray-load loss does IEEE 112 assign to a 300 HP motor?
back: 1.5%, from the 125 to 500 HP band. The other bands are: 1 to 125 HP 1.8%; 501 to 2499 HP 1.2%; 2500 HP and above 0.9%.
explain: IEEE 112 is the detailed method and is rarely used on the shop floor. IS and IEC standards use a flat 0.5% of input instead.

front: What stray-load loss do IS and IEC motor standards assume, and how does the actual value compare?
back: A fixed 0.5% of input power. The actual stray loss is likely higher, about 1 to 3% for motors up to 200 HP.
explain: Stray losses are hard to measure, so the standard value understates total losses. This is why efficiency figures based on IEEE methods come out lower.

front: Can two test methods, or two manufacturers, give different efficiency figures for the same motor?
back: Yes. The same motor can differ by about 2% between test methods, or between manufacturers using the same method.
explain: The chapter advises asking for detailed test certificates, specifying efficiency without tolerance, and relying on measured input current and kW rather than labelled values.

front: How is rotor I²R loss estimated in the field?
back: Rotor I²R loss = slip × (stator input − stator I²R loss − core loss).
explain: Slip is measured with a stroboscope or non-contact tachometer. The chapter also requires the slip to be corrected to operating temperature.

front: A 34 kW, 415 V, 57 A, 1475 rpm delta motor has stator resistance 0.264 Ω per phase at 30 °C. Its no-load test gives 415 V, 16.1 A and 1063.74 W. Estimate its full-load efficiency and full-load power factor.
back: Full-load efficiency about 92.2%; full-load PF about 0.90. Iron plus friction and windage about 995 W; stator I²R at 120 °C about 1150 W; slip 1.67%; motor input about 36.9 kW.
explain: This is the chapter's field estimation method, which uses measured values for every calculation. Nameplate efficiency is used only for comparison.

steps.explain: At no load the input supplies only stator I²R, core loss and friction and windage, so subtracting the stator copper loss leaves the fixed losses.

steps.explain: Modern motors run at 100 to 120 °C, so the 30 °C reading must be corrected upward before running losses are calculated.

steps.explain: Stator I²R uses the hot resistance and the full-load line current.

steps.explain: Rotor input is shaft output divided by (1 − slip), because rotor losses equal slip times rotor input.

steps.explain: Standards assume stray losses of 0.5%. The chapter notes actual values are often 1 to 3%, so this estimate is optimistic.

steps.explain: Power factor is real input divided by apparent input, using the measured current. The result is only as good as the test data behind it.

front: What efficiency tolerance does IS 325 allow on standard motors?
back: 15% tolerance on efficiency for motors up to 50 kW, and 10% for motors above 50 kW.
explain: A labelled efficiency can therefore sit well below the true value. Buyers should ask for test certificates rather than rely on labelled values.

front: Why can the cheapest motor end up costing the most?
back: A low-cost motor usually has lower efficiency, so its running cost over life is higher. An efficient motor often saves several times its extra cost within a few years.
explain: Buyers should also check the power drawn at 75% loading and the reactive kVAr drawn, both useful selection indicators. Being first-cost sensitive is a common reason for poor lifecycle economics.

front: What share of total motor losses do stator and rotor I²R losses typically make up?
back: About 55 to 60%. Core losses make up 20 to 25%, friction and windage 8 to 12%, and stray load losses 4 to 5%.
explain: Stator I²R falls with more copper and larger conductors, and rotor I²R falls with larger or copper rotor bars. Operating closer to synchronous speed also reduces rotor losses.

front: How much higher is the full-load efficiency of an energy-efficient motor than that of a standard motor?
back: About 3 to 7% higher. Mounting dimensions are kept to IS 1231 so the motor can replace the old one easily.
explain: Energy-efficient motors use design changes such as lower-loss steel, longer cores, thicker wires, copper rotor bars and a smaller air gap. Their higher price is usually recovered quickly through operating savings.

front: Name three situations where energy-efficient motors are generally poorly suited.
back: Highly intermittent or special torque duties such as hoists, cranes, traction drives, punch presses, machine tools and centrifuges; applications needing multi-speed motors; and duties where the motor runs only on continuous duty cycles.
explain: Their economics depend on savings from running hours, so they pay back least where the motor runs rarely. They are most attractive in new applications or at end-of-life replacement.

front: What service factor and design loading does the chapter recommend for energy-efficient motors?
back: A 1.15 service factor, with the motor designed to operate at about 85% of rated load.
explain: Poor incoming power quality can affect energy-efficient motors. They also run about 1% faster than standard motors because of their lower slip.

front: What supply variation must a standard Indian motor tolerate under BIS?
back: It must deliver rated output with ±6% voltage variation and ±3% frequency variation.
explain: Fluctuations larger than these are common in utility supply in India, and voltage fluctuations affect motor performance. Voltage unbalance is a separate issue, recommended at 1% or less.

front: What is the recommended maximum voltage unbalance at motor terminals?
back: 1%. Above this, the motor must be derated.
explain: Voltage unbalance is probably the leading power factor problem behind motor overheating and premature failure. Current imbalance can be 6 to 10 times the voltage imbalance.

back: About 1.29%, which is above the 1% recommended limit, so the motor would need derating.
explain: NEMA defines unbalance from the mean of the three line voltages and the largest single deviation. Unequal single-phase loads and unequal cable impedance are common causes.

steps.explain: NEMA measures unbalance relative to the average of the three line voltages.

back: About 3.3 °C, using additional temperature rise = 2 × (% voltage unbalance)².
explain: The chapter's own example uses a 2% unbalance at 100 °C, which gives an 8 °C rise. Insulation life halves for each 10 °C rise, so even a small unbalance matters.
