front: How is percentage motor loading estimated, and what is the common mistake?
back: % loading = measured input kW ÷ (rated kW ÷ rated efficiency) × 100. Never assume the power factor, and do not estimate loading as the ratio of currents.
explain: The current ratio ignores changes in power factor and efficiency at part load. Measuring kW input directly gives a reliable loading figure.

front: Why is under-loading a common cause of poor motor efficiency?
back: It lowers both efficiency and power factor and raises first cost. Replacing motors running at 60 to 70% of capacity or higher is generally not recommended.
explain: Causes include large OEM safety factors, equipment that rarely needs full capacity, oversizing to hold output at low voltage, and oversizing for high starting torque. Each case needs its own evaluation.

front: How does the chapter suggest choosing a motor rating for a variable load?
back: Use the load duration curve: pick a rating whose continuous full-load temperature rise equals the weighted average temperature rise over the cycle. A rating slightly below peak load can then run briefly overloaded.
explain: This method underestimates heating for frequent starts and stops or high-inertia loads, so it should not be used for those duties.

front: What is the maximum capacitor size that should be connected across a motor?
back: No more than 90% of the motor's no-load kVAr. Larger capacitors can cause over-voltage and motor burn-out.
explain: No-load kVAr is found from a no-load test. If testing is not possible, standard power factor values for typical motors give a conservative estimate.

front: Does a power factor capacitor fitted at a motor's starter improve the motor's own operating power factor?
back: No. It improves the power factor upstream, from the capacitor back to the generating side, not the motor's own operating PF.
explain: Upstream benefits include lower kVA demand, lower I²R losses in cables and reduced voltage drop. The largest overall system gain comes when the capacitor is across the motor terminals.

front: What usually happens to a motor's efficiency after rewinding?
back: It usually falls. Careful rewinding can keep it at the earlier level, and with proper design measures it can sometimes be improved.
explain: Over 50% of motors in some industries have been rewound. Stripping old windings with heat damages lamination insulation and raises eddy current losses, and a smaller wire diameter raises resistance and I²R losses.

front: What simple record shows whether a rewound motor was rewound well?
back: A log of no-load input current for each motor. A rising no-load current indicates a poor-quality rewind.
explain: Keep the no-load input power and speed from the time of purchase so the effect of rewinding can be checked. Reviewing the rewind shop's procedures also gives an indication of quality.

front: What is the difference between constant-torque and variable-torque loads, with examples?
back: Constant torque: conveyors, rotary kilns and constant-displacement pumps, where torque stays the same across speed. Variable torque: centrifugal pumps and fans, where torque varies with the square of speed.
explain: Power in variable torque loads varies with the cube of speed, so VSDs save the most energy there. Machine tools are a typical constant-power load, where torque falls as speed rises.

front: What speed options does a multi-speed motor offer?
back: A single winding gives two speeds in a 2:1 ratio. Two separate windings give four speeds in total.
explain: Multi-speed motors suit applications needing two or four fixed speeds rather than continuous speed control, and they are economical for that. They have lower efficiency than single-speed motors.

front: When is slip power recovery an economical speed control method?
back: Only in relatively high-power applications where the motor speed range is 1:5 or less.
explain: It is used with slip-ring motors. Instead of wasting slip power in resistors, it returns the excess power from the slip rings to the shaft or the supply line.

front: Why does a VFD change voltage together with frequency rather than frequency alone?
back: To keep the magnetic flux nearly constant, so torque stays nearly constant up to base speed. Above base speed the voltage cannot rise, so the flux weakens and torque falls.
explain: Lowering frequency alone would raise the flux and could saturate the core. This constant V/f control is the most popular VFD control method in industry.

front: How does a fluid coupling vary the speed of driven equipment without changing the motor speed?
back: It works on the hydrodynamic principle: oil carries power from the impeller on the motor side to the runner on the load side. A speed difference (slip) is needed for the oil to flow.
explain: Maximum torque occurs at standstill and sets the limiting torque, so the coupling also acts as a torque limiter. A fusible plug drains the oil on sustained overload.

front: Which efficiency classes are used in the star labelling scheme for energy-efficient induction motors?
back: IE2, IE2(+), IE3, IE3(+) and IE3(++), based on IS 12615:2011. The scheme covers 2, 4 and 6 pole continuous duty motors rated 0.37 to 375 kW.
explain: The schedule sets the rated output, efficiency class, label validity requirements, performance criteria, test report format and label design. It is run under the BEE S & L programme on energy-efficient motors.

front: A 50 HP, 415 V, 60 A, 1475 rpm, delta-connected standard motor shows 415 V, 18 A and 1080 W at no load (50 Hz), with 0.27 Ω stator resistance per phase. Estimate the iron plus friction and windage losses, full-load stator copper loss at 120 °C, slip, motor input, and full-load efficiency and PF. Take stray loss as 0.5% of rated output.
back: Iron + F&W about 992.5 W; R₁₂₀ about 0.355 Ω; stator I²R about 1278 W; slip 1.67%; rotor input about 37.9 kW; motor input about 40.4 kW; efficiency about 92.3%; PF about 0.94.
explain: This follows the same method as the chapter's worked example. The 0.27 Ω reading is assumed to be taken at the 35 °C ambient, which should be checked against the test record.

steps.prompt: Find the stator I²R loss at no load and the iron plus friction and windage losses.
steps.explain: No-load input minus stator copper loss leaves the core and friction and windage losses.
The 35 °C ambient is assumed as the reference temperature of the 0.27 Ω reading.

steps.prompt: Find the full-load stator copper loss at 120 °C.
steps.explain: Hot resistance and full-load current give the operating-temperature copper loss.

steps.prompt: Find the slip and the rotor input.
steps.explain: 1 HP = 746 W, and rotor input = output ÷ (1 − slip).
Stray loss is taken at the standard 0.5% of rated output.

steps.prompt: Find the full-load efficiency and power factor.
steps.explain: Efficiency is output over input, and PF is input kW over the apparent power at full-load current.

front: What share of the prime mover's energy reaches the point of end-use in a compressed air system?
back: Only about 10–30%. The remaining 70–90% is lost as unusable heat, with smaller losses to friction, misuse and noise.
explain: Figure 3.1 is a Sankey diagram of this energy flow. The book's message is that simple, cost-effective measures on the demand side can save around 30%.

front: Name the two broad classes of air compressor.
back: Positive displacement compressors (pressure raised by reducing volume) and dynamic compressors (air velocity converted into pressure).
explain: Positive displacement machines are reciprocating or rotary. Dynamic machines are centrifugal, either radial or axial flow. Flow and pressure requirements decide which type suits a given application.

front: What are the four most widely used reciprocating compressor configurations?
back: Horizontal, vertical, horizontal balance-opposed and tandem.
explain: Vertical units cover about 50–150 cfm. Horizontal balance-opposed units cover 200–5000 cfm in multi-stage designs and up to 10,000 cfm in single-stage designs.

front: What discharge temperatures do two-stage and single-stage reciprocating compressors reach?
back: Two-stage: about 140–160°C. Single-stage: about 205–240°C.
explain: Two-stage machines are used for high pressures. Their lower discharge temperature is one reason multi-stage units can have lower specific power than single-stage units over the same pressure range.

front: What is the most common rotary air compressor, and how does it compress air?
back: The single-stage helical or spiral oil-flooded screw compressor. Two rotors compress air inside a casing with no valves. Oil seals the clearances and cools the air, and must be separated from the discharge air.
explain: Cooling takes place inside the compressor, so the working parts never see extreme temperatures. Oil-free screw types also exist, using specially designed air ends.

front: Why is the reported isothermal efficiency of a compressor usually lower than its adiabatic efficiency?
back: Isothermal power excludes the power needed to overcome friction, so isothermal efficiency comes out lower. Manufacturers usually report the isothermal figure, so check the basis before comparing machines.
explain: Both figures measure overall efficiency, covering the compressor and its drive motor. The book flags this as an important consideration when selecting compressors from reported efficiency values.

front: Isothermal power is P₁ × Q × ln(r) / 36.7 kW, with P₁ and P₂ in kg/cm² absolute, Q free air in m³/h and r = P₂/P₁. Find the isothermal power for a 1000 m³/h FAD compressing from 1.0 to 8.0 kg/cm² abs, and its isothermal efficiency if the motor input is 70 kW.
back: About 56.7 kW of isothermal power, giving an isothermal efficiency of about 81%.
explain: The 36.7 divisor absorbs the unit conversion for kg/cm² and m³/h. Isothermal power is the ideal minimum work for the duty, so dividing by measured input gives the overall efficiency of compressor and motor.

steps.explain: Both pressures must be absolute for the book's formula.
The formula uses the natural logarithm (the OCR shows it as log_e r).
Q is free air delivered in m³/h, not m³/min.

steps.prompt: Compute the isothermal efficiency with a 70 kW motor input.
steps.explain: Isothermal efficiency is isothermal power divided by actual measured input power.

front: Name the major components of a compressed air system.
back: Intake air filters, inter-stage coolers, after-coolers, air dryers, moisture drain traps, receivers, piping network, filters, regulators and lubricators.
explain: Filters keep dust out of the compressor, coolers remove heat and moisture, dryers supply dry air for instruments, and receivers damp pulsation and store air. Regulators and lubricators sit as close as possible to the equipment they serve.

front: What is the thumb rule for compressor inlet air temperature?
back: Every 4°C drop in inlet air temperature lowers energy consumption by about 1% for the same output.
explain: The compressor room runs warmer than ambient because of compression heat, so draw cool air from outside. Use a large-diameter suction duct with few bends to limit pressure drop on the intake.

front: How much does a 250 mm WC pressure drop across a choked intake filter raise compressor power?
back: About 2% for the same output. Table 3.4 gives 1.6% at 200 mm WC, 3.2% at 400, 4.7% at 600 and 7.0% at 800 mm WC.
explain: Fit manometers or differential pressure gauges across the filter to plan cleaning and replacement. Choose the filter for the compressor type and install it as close to the compressor as possible.

front: How much water vapour does 1000 m³/min of air at 30°C carry at 100% relative humidity, according to Table 3.5?
back: About 68.22 kg per hour. The table gives 45.00 kg/h at 80% RH and 27.60 kg/h at 50% RH.
explain: Moisture carrying capacity rises with temperature and falls with pressure. Intake near a cooling tower or a dryer exhaust adds moisture, so the book says to avoid it.

front: Table 3.8 gives a minimum cooling water flow of 18.9 L/min for a two-stage compressor with after-cooler at 2.85 m³/min FAD and 7 bar. Estimate the minimum for a 5.7 m³/min machine of the same type, assuming flow scales linearly with FAD.
back: About 37.8 L/min. This is an estimate; the book gives only the 2.85 m³/min figure.
explain: Linear scaling is an assumption made for this exercise, not a rule stated in the book. Confirm cooling water needs with the compressor maker's data, since both too little flow and too cold water cause problems.

steps.explain: The reference machine in Table 3.8 is 2.85 m³/min.

steps.prompt: Scale the minimum cooling water flow.
steps.explain: Assumes linear scaling with FAD at the same 7 bar.

steps.prompt: State the check before sizing the pump.
steps.answer: Verify against the compressor maker's cooling water data.
steps.explain: The book warns that very low cooling water temperature can condense moisture in the air and damage cylinders.

front: A compressor is set at 6–7 kg/cm². At what pressures does it load and unload?
back: It loads (cuts in) at 6 kg/cm² and unloads (cuts out) at 7 kg/cm², with a pressure switch doing the switching.
explain: The book says cut-in and cut-out should be set at optimum levels, and the gap between them kept as narrow as practical.

front: How much input power does a 1 bar reduction in delivery pressure save?
back: About 6–10%. The book's example: cutting delivery from 8 to 7 kg/cm² saves about 9% of input power.
explain: Before lowering the setting, study the pressure needs of each equipment and the pressure drop between generation and use. Lower delivery pressure also gives better volumetric efficiency.

front: Several compressors feed one header. Which one should be the modulating compressor?
back: If sizes differ, only the smallest compressor modulates. If types differ, the one with the lowest no-load or part-load power modulates, and the others run near full load.
explain: Grade compressors by specific energy consumption at each pressure, and let the most efficient ones carry most of the demand.

front: Five reciprocating compressors (A to E) serve one plant section on a 45-minute cycle. A to D run full time and E loads for 5.88 min. Capacities at 7 kg/cm² are 13.17, 12.32, 13.14, 12.75 and 13.65 m³/min. Find the air generated on line, the consumption rate and the air drawl as a percentage of capacity on line.
back: Capacity on line is 2926.35 m³ per cycle. Air consumed is 2392.36 m³ per cycle, or 53.16 m³/min. Air drawl is 81.75%.
explain: The section draws only about four-fifths of what the compressors could make. The book suggests keeping one compressor in cycling mode and replacing the one with the highest unload losses with a smaller unit.

steps.prompt: Find the capacity on line for the 45-minute cycle.
steps.explain: Each machine's capacity is multiplied by the full cycle time, as the book does.

steps.prompt: Find the air actually drawn (consumed) per cycle.
steps.explain: Compressor E only contributes for its 5.88 min of loading, not the full cycle.
Cycle output divided by cycle length gives the average rate the section draws.

steps.prompt: Find the air drawl as a percentage of capacity on line.
steps.explain: The remaining 18.25% is capacity the section does not use.

front: What pressure drop is acceptable in the mains header at the farthest point, and in the distribution system?
back: 0.3 bar in the mains header at the farthest point, and 0.5 bar in the distribution system.
explain: Excess drop from small pipe, choked filters or undersized couplings forces a higher generation pressure and wastes power. The design limit from compressor to the most distant point of use is 5%.

front: Table 3.11 gives a power loss of 9.5 kW for 170 m³/h (100 cfm) through a 40 mm bore pipe, and 1.2 kW through a 65 mm bore pipe. At 8000 h/yr and Rs 5/kWh (the book's basis), what is the annual saving from upsizing 40 mm to 65 mm?
back: About 8.3 kW, or 66,400 kWh and about Rs 3.3 lakh per year, before the cost of the larger pipe.
explain: The book says present energy prices justify liberal pipe sizing to reduce pressure drop. An undersized bore wastes energy every hour it runs, so the saving recurs each year.

steps.prompt: Find the power saved per hour.
steps.explain: Table 3.11 gives the equivalent power loss for the stated flow in each pipe size.
Uses the 8000 operating hours assumed in the book's leakage cost table.
Rs 5/kWh is the book's tariff assumption. The extra pipe cost must be netted off to find the payback.

front: What are the main capacity control methods for compressors, and what do they cost in power?
back: On/off control (best for small units, as motor idle losses are eliminated); load/unload (unloaded power up to 30% of full load); multi-step (0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% steps); throttling or speed control for centrifugal units.
explain: Table 3.13 shows a typical reciprocating machine at about 80% of full-load power at 75% load, 60% at 50% load and 40% at 25% load.

front: Above what share of system volume does speed control beat vane control for a centrifugal compressor?
back: Above about 40% of system volume, speed control is recommended. Below 40%, vane control can draw less power.
explain: Below 40% the speed control system itself becomes inefficient, which is why vane control can win at very low flow. Vane control works through adjustable inlet guide vanes.

front: A paper plant conveyed wood chips with compressed air at an equivalent 77 kW. A blower now does the job at 7 kW. What is the saving in kW and in percent, and the annual energy saved at 8000 h/yr?
back: 70 kW saved, about 91% of the original power. That is 560,000 kWh/yr at 8000 h/yr.
explain: The book uses this case to show that blower conveying is far cheaper than compressed air for low-pressure material handling.

steps.explain: Same conveying duty, different air supply.
Compares the saving with the original compressed air load.
Uses the 8000 operating hours that the book assumes in its leakage cost example.

front: What is the book's guidance on using compressed air for cleaning or blowing dust?
back: Use blowers or local fans for moving air where possible. If compressed air is unavoidable, use blow guns and keep pressure below 2 bar. A 1/4 inch hose left open at 7 bar for 1000 h/yr costs about Rs 1 lakh per year.
explain: Misuse such as body cleaning, floor cleaning and liquid agitation should be discouraged. Where cleaning air is essential, use a separate cleaning header with a main isolation valve opened only for defined periods.

front: What does a 3.1 mm orifice leak waste, and what does it cost per year, according to Table 3.17?
back: About 3.0 kW, costing about Rs 1.2 lakh per year (Rs 120,000) at Rs 5/kWh, 8000 h/yr and 7 bar.
explain: Even small leaks are costly: a 0.8 mm orifice wastes 0.2 kW (Rs 8000/yr). The book says the cost of stopping leaks is repaid through energy savings.

front: A 35 m³/min compressor cycles with all users closed: average load time 1.5 min, unload time 10.5 min, and 188 kW drawn on load. Find the leakage rate, leakage per day, specific power of generation and energy lost to leakage per day.
back: Leakage 4.375 m³/min, or 6300 m³/day. Specific power 0.0895 kWh/m³. Energy lost to leakage about 564 kWh/day.
explain: The leak fraction is load time over total cycle time, applied to rated capacity. Leaked air still costs full compression energy, so the loss is a daily cost.

steps.explain: Leak fraction is the on-load time over the total cycle time.
Converts the per-minute rate to a 24-hour day.

steps.prompt: Find the specific power for compressed air generation.
steps.explain: Full-load power divided by hourly delivery gives energy per cubic metre.

steps.prompt: Find the energy lost to leakage per day.
steps.explain: Leaked volume times specific power gives the daily energy wasted.

front: How much moisture does an aftercooler remove, and what happens to the rest?
back: About 60–75% of the moisture is removed at the after-cooler. The rest condenses as the air cools in the lines, which is enough for cleaning and atomisation but not for instrument or pneumatic use.
explain: Remaining vapour must be taken out by air dryers for instrumentation and pneumatics. Warm, humid air reaching the receivers increases condensation, corrosion and leakage.

front: Air at an atmospheric dew point of −10°C and 1013.3 mbar holds water vapour at 2.8 mbar partial pressure. It is compressed to 2026.6 mbar. What are the new vapour partial pressure and the approximate dew point?
back: Vapour partial pressure doubles to 5.6 mbar. The dew point rises to about −1°C.
explain: Compression raises the dew point, so a dryer's performance is quoted as a pressure dew point, which is higher than the atmospheric figure.

steps.explain: Total pressure doubles.

steps.prompt: Find the new water vapour partial pressure (Dalton's law).
steps.explain: With the same moisture content, the partial pressure of vapour scales with total pressure.
The book quotes approximately −1°C as the temperature at which 5.6 mbar of vapour condenses.

front: How does a refrigerant dryer lower the dew point, and what dew point does it reach?
back: It chills the air so moisture condenses out. A second heat exchanger has the outgoing cold air pre-cool the incoming air. Atmospheric dew point reaches about −20°C.
explain: It is the most economical dryer for about 90% of applications. It removes almost 100% of solid particles and water droplets larger than 3 µm.

front: How does a heat of compression (HOC) desiccant dryer regenerate its desiccant without an external heat source?
back: It uses hot air taken straight from the compressor discharge, about 135°C from a reciprocating machine, before the after-cooler. No electric heater is fitted and there is no purge loss, so operating cost is zero or very low.
explain: HOC dryers serve about 400 to 5000 cfm. Each vessel is in service for 4 hours while the other regenerates: 2.5 hours heating and 1.5 hours cooling.

front: What is the purge loss of a heatless purge desiccant dryer, and below what capacity is it used?
back: About 12–15% of the dry air is used for purging, so operating cost is very high. It is used for capacities below about 250 cfm.
explain: Blower-reactivated dryers, used above 250 cfm, lose about 1–2% to purge but need a heater. HOC dryers have no purge loss at all.

front: What are the functions of an air receiver?
back: It dampens pulsation from the compressor, acts as a reservoir for sudden demand above compressor capacity, prevents short cycling, and lets moisture carried over from the after-coolers settle out.
explain: Place a receiver near a load with sudden, short-lived high demand to avoid adding compressor capacity. The book wants receivers generously sized for a large cooling surface.

front: Using the IS 7938 rule of thumb quoted in the book, what receiver volume suits a compressor delivering 12 m³/min?
back: Between 1.2 m³ and 2.0 m³, that is one-tenth to one-sixth of the output per minute.
explain: The book wants the receiver generously sized to give a large cooling surface and to even out pulsation from a reciprocating compressor.

steps.explain: One-tenth of the output in m³/min.
One-sixth of the output in m³/min.

steps.prompt: Pick a size within the range.
steps.answer: Any volume from 1.2 to 2.0 m³; the larger end gives more cooling surface and smoother pressure.
steps.explain: The rule is a range, not a single answer, so the choice depends on the load pattern.

front: What air velocity range is usual in compressed air mains, and why?
back: 6 to 10 m/s. This keeps pressure drop low on most systems and lets moisture precipitate.
explain: Pipe size is chosen from the allowable velocity and then checked against pressure drop. Mains should slope down toward a dead end, with traps at all low points.

front: Size a compressed air main for 200 cfm (5.66 m³/min free air) delivered at 7.0 kg/cm² gauge, with a velocity limit of 6 m/s. What is the pipe bore?
back: About 0.0538 m (53.8 mm), so a 2 inch nominal bore pipe is chosen.
explain: The book uses 7.0 directly in the gas-law step. The method is area equals flow divided by velocity, then diameter from the circle area.

steps.explain: Constant-temperature gas law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, as the book applies it.
Velocity is in m/s, so flow must be in m³/s.
Area equals flow divided by allowable velocity.

steps.answer: D = √(4A / π) = 0.0538 m, about 2.11 inch. Choose 2 inch nominal bore.
steps.explain: Round up to the next standard nominal bore.

front: What share of capacity or efficiency can a worn compressor valve cost?
back: A worn valve can cut capacity by as much as 20% (Section 3.6). The checklist warns that worn valves can reduce efficiency by as much as 50%, so inspect valves about every six months.
explain: The two figures come from different parts of the chapter, so answer with the one the question asks for and note the difference. A periodic FAD test reveals the loss, and deviations above 10% need corrective action.

front: A pump-up test uses a total storage volume of 8.287 m³ (receiver 7.79 m³ plus 0.4974 m³ hold-up). Pressure rises from 0.5 to 7.03 kg/cm² in 4.021 min, atmospheric is 1.026 kg/cm² abs, and rated capacity is 14.75 m³/min. Find the output and the shortfall.
back: Output about 13.12 m³/min. Shortfall 1.63 m³/min, or 11.05%, so the compressor needs investigation.
explain: The formula assumes the discharge air is at ambient temperature (perfect isothermal compression). If discharge air is hotter, multiply by (273 + ambient) / (273 + discharge) as the book describes.

steps.explain: Receiver plus additional hold-up volume in the pipe and cooler.
Pressure rise times volume, divided by atmospheric pressure times pump-up time.

steps.prompt: Find the shortfall against the rating.
steps.explain: The rated capacity is 14.75 m³/min at 7 kg/cm².
A deviation above 10% calls for corrective measures.

front: Why are ball, plug or gate valves preferred over globe valves in compressed air lines?
back: Globe valves cause a high pressure drop, so ball, plug or gate valves are preferred.
explain: Fittings also create pressure loss, quantified as equivalent lengths in Table 3.12. Welded joints in place of screwed or flexible joints reduce both leakage and pressure drop.

front: How much more energy do pneumatic transport and pneumatic tools use compared with mechanical or electric alternatives?
back: Pneumatic transport uses about 8 times more energy than mechanical systems. Pneumatic drills and grinders use about 20 times more than motor-driven tools.
explain: Table 3.15 shows a pneumatic jet grinder at 3.59 kW against 0.18 kW for an electric straight grinder, about 20 times. Safety overrides energy saving, so electric tools are not allowed where flammable vapours are present.

front: How much of a plant's compressed air can leakage account for, and what is the first step?
back: Leakage of 40–50% is not uncommon. The first step is periodic leak tests to estimate the quantity lost.
explain: Leaks mostly occur at receivers, relief valves, pipe and hose joints, shut-off valves, quick-release couplings and tools, usually from poor maintenance or poor installation.

front: In an automobile plant, a pump-up test uses a 4100 L receiver and piping volume. Pressure rises from 1 to 8.5 kg/cm² gauge in 65 s. Atmospheric is 1.026 kg/cm² abs, ambient 32°C and final air temperature 52°C. Find the FAD in m³/min and in cfm.
back: About 25.96 m³/min, or about 916 cfm.
explain: Hot discharge air is corrected back to ambient conditions with the temperature ratio, which lowers the raw output of 27.66 m³/min by about 6%.

steps.explain: The formula works in m³ and minutes.
Gauge pressure rise divided by atmospheric pressure.
Pressure term times volume, divided by pump-up time.
Converts the hot discharge air back to ambient inlet conditions.
One cubic metre per minute is about 35.3 cfm.

front: On the same system and compressor (FAD 916 cfm), a leakage test with no pneumatic equipment running shows 3 min on load and 13 min unloaded, with 145 kW drawn on load. Find the leakage percentage, the leakage in cfm, the specific power and the power lost to leakage.
back: 18.75%; 171.75 cfm; 0.1583 kW/cfm; about 27.19 kW lost.
explain: The leak fraction is load time over the total cycle. The leak flow then carries the compressor's specific power with it, which gives the power wasted.

steps.explain: Load time as a fraction of the total cycle.
Applies the leak fraction to the FAD.
Full-load power per cfm of delivered air.

steps.prompt: Find the power lost to leakage.
steps.explain: Leak flow times specific power.

front: A receiver of 0.3 m³, plus 0.05 m³ of hold-up pipe and cooler, is pumped from 0 to 7 kg/cm² gauge in 4.1 min. Air temperature rises from 35°C to 50°C. Atmospheric is 1.026 kg/cm² abs. Find the FAD in m³/h.
back: About 33 m³/h (0.555 m³/min).
explain: This is the same pump-up method as the worked examples. The temperature ratio corrects the hotter discharge air back to inlet conditions.

steps.explain: Receiver plus hold-up volume.
Gauge pressure rise divided by atmospheric pressure.
Pressure term times volume, divided by pump-up time.
Converts discharge air at 50°C back to the 35°C inlet reference.
Multiply m³/min by 60 for the hourly FAD.

front: What is refrigeration, in terms of heat transfer?
back: The removal and relocation of heat: it moves heat from a low-temperature source to a high-temperature sink, using a low-boiling refrigerant.
explain: Heat does not flow from cold to hot naturally, so external energy (electricity or heat) must drive mechanical equipment to do it. The refrigerant is chosen because it boils at a low temperature, absorbing heat from the cold side.

front: Name the five heat transfer loops in an HVAC and refrigeration system, from the indoor space to the outdoors.
back: 1) Indoor air loop (supply air fan through the cooling coil); 2) chilled water loop (pump returns water from the coil to the chiller evaporator); 3) refrigerant loop (compressor pumps heat to the condenser water); 4) condenser water loop (pump sends heat to the cooling tower); 5) cooling tower loop (fan drives air across the hot water to the outdoors).
explain: Thermal energy moves through these five loops in sequence, each passing the heat to the next. Tracing the loop order helps locate where a fault or inefficiency sits in the system.

front: Name five properties of air that a psychrometric chart shows.
back: Any five of: dry-bulb temperature, wet-bulb temperature, dew point, specific humidity, relative humidity, enthalpy (kJ/kg dry air), specific volume (m³/kg).
explain: The chart shows these properties on one diagram. It lets an engineer turn a heating or cooling load in kW or TR into an air volume flow in m³/s or cfm for the duct system.

front: What are the specific humidity, enthalpy, wet-bulb temperature, dew point and specific volume of air at 32°C dry-bulb and 60% RH?
back: About 18 g moisture/kg dry air; 78 kJ/kg dry air; wet-bulb 25.5°C; dew point 23°C; specific volume 0.89 m³/kg.
explain: This is the book's chart-reading example (Figure 4.2). Reading the chart correctly needs the dry-bulb line and the 60% RH curve to cross exactly. Practise reading all five values from one point.

steps.prompt: Locate 32°C on the dry-bulb axis and move up to the 60% RH curve.
steps.answer: That intersection is the air state point.
steps.explain: Every property is read from this single point.

steps.prompt: Read the specific humidity at that point.
steps.answer: About 18 g moisture per kg of dry air (0.018 kg/kg).
steps.explain: Specific humidity is the mass of water vapour per mass of dry air.

steps.prompt: Read the enthalpy at that point.
steps.explain: Enthalpy is the total heat content, used for cooling and heating loads.

steps.prompt: Read the wet-bulb temperature, dew point and specific volume.
steps.answer: Wet-bulb about 25.5°C; dew point about 23°C; specific volume about 0.89 m³/kg.
steps.explain: Specific volume converts a mass flow into a volume flow for the ducts.

front: What is the human comfort zone on a psychrometric chart?
back: Dry-bulb temperature 22–27°C with relative humidity 40–60%.
explain: Most people feel comfortable inside this zone. Air conditioning uses the chart to decide whether air must be heated or cooled, humidified or dehumidified to bring it into the zone.

front: Outdoor air at 35°C and 60% RH is cooled and reheated to 24°C and 53% RH. How much moisture is removed, how much heat is removed, and how much heat is added?
back: Moisture removed about 11.5 g/kg dry air; heat removed about 48 kJ/kg dry air (cooling); heat added about 10 kJ/kg dry air (reheating).
explain: Cooling below the dew point condenses moisture, and reheating raises the temperature without changing moisture. The book labels the states 1 (outdoor air), 2 (saturated, 100% RH) and 3 (comfort zone).

steps.prompt: Plot state 1: 35°C dry bulb at 60% RH.
steps.answer: This is the outdoor air state.
steps.explain: The process starts from the outdoor condition.

steps.prompt: Find the moisture removed between state 1 and the saturated state 2.
steps.answer: About 11.5 g moisture removed per kg of dry air.
steps.explain: The moisture falls out as liquid when the air is cooled to saturation.

steps.prompt: Find the heat removed in the cooling step (1 to 2).
steps.explain: This is the enthalpy difference across the cooling coil.

steps.prompt: Plot state 3 at 24°C and 53% RH, then find the heat added in reheating (2 to 3).
steps.explain: Reheating raises the temperature at constant moisture content.

front: What drives vapour compression refrigeration (VCR) and what drives vapour absorption refrigeration (VAR)?
back: VCR is driven by mechanical energy (a compressor); VAR is driven by thermal energy (steam, hot water, gas, oil or waste heat).
explain: Both move heat from low to high temperature. VAR still needs some electricity for its pumps, which is why it suits sites with waste heat.

front: What are small, medium and large refrigeration plant capacities in TR?
back: Small: up to 50 TR; medium: 50–250 TR; large: over 250 TR.
explain: The book uses these bands when comparing plant options. A large industry may run a bank of such units, sharing chilled water pumps, condenser pumps and cooling towers as an off-site utility.

front: Is the absorber a component of a vapour compression refrigeration cycle?
back: No. A VCR cycle uses a compressor, condenser, expansion device and evaporator. The absorber belongs to absorption (VAR) systems.
explain: In VAR, refrigerant vapour is absorbed into a lithium bromide solution in the absorber. Exam questions often use the absorber as a trap option in VCR lists.

front: What did the Montreal Protocol (1987) require for CFC refrigerants, and when did India complete its CFC phase-out?
back: A phased reduction in ozone-depleting CFC production, with an eventual stop by 1996. India completed the CFC phase-out on 1 August 2008.
explain: The Copenhagen agreement (1992) followed. CFCs damage the ozone layer, so the industry moved to HCFCs and then HFCs. Keep the years 1987, 1996 and 2008 in mind for exam questions.

front: What is the HCFC phase-out schedule for Article 5 parties under the 19th Meeting of Parties (MOP)?
back: Base level is the average of 2009 and 2010. Freeze at base level in 2013; 10% reduction in 2015; 35% in 2020; 67.5% in 2025; 100% in 2030, followed by a 2.5% average annual service tail in 2030–2040.
explain: The 19th MOP accelerated the phase-out of HCFC production and consumption. The schedule is dated, so confirm current figures with the Ministry of Environment and Forests (Ozone Cell) before relying on it.

front: What is the typical COP of a Li-Br–water absorption chiller, and what chilled water temperature can it give with 30°C cooling water?
back: COP 0.65–0.70; it gives chilled water at 6.7°C. Systems giving chilled water at 3°C are also available.
explain: This COP is thermal: cooling output per unit of heat input. It should not be compared directly with the electric COP of a compression chiller.

front: Why can older centrifugal compressors not reduce load much below about 50%?
back: Surge: as flow is choked off, the gas does not gain enough energy to overcome discharge pressure. Flow drops abruptly, the gas oscillates back and forth in the impeller, efficiency falls and vibration can damage the machine.
explain: Many older machines handle low loads with hot gas bypass, which wastes the unneeded cooling output. Newer machines combine variable-speed drives with inlet guide vanes to reach about 20% load.

front: How do screw compressors usually control capacity, and when can a variable-speed drive be used on them?
back: Usually with a slide valve forming part of the housing around the screws. A variable-speed drive is limited to oil-injected compressors, because slowing a dry compressor allows excessive internal leakage.
explain: Screw compressors suit higher condensing pressures, such as with HCFC-22 and ammonia, and are compact. Part-load efficiency depends strongly on the capacity control method used.

front: What four power inputs make up the overall kW/TR of a centralised chilled water plant?
back: Compressor, chilled water pump, condenser water pump and cooling tower fan. The overall kW/TR is the sum of the kW/TR of each.
explain: Compressor power alone understates the true plant energy use. Pump and fan power must be added to get the total specific power consumption.

front: What is the ideal (Carnot) COP for an evaporator at -15°C and a condenser at 30°C?
back: About 5.7 (5.74), using absolute temperatures: 258.15 / (303.15 − 258.15).
explain: The Carnot COP is an upper limit set only by the two temperatures. Real compressors have lower COP because of losses, so the book uses the actual cooling effect divided by compressor input for industry COP.

steps.explain: Carnot formulas need absolute temperatures.
The lift is the condenser temperature minus the evaporator temperature.
Higher evaporator temperature or lower condenser temperature raises this value.

steps.explain: The Carnot figure ignores compressor type, so it is a benchmark, not a prediction.

front: What parameters must be measured to estimate chiller performance in kW/TR?
back: Chilled water inlet and outlet temperatures (instrument least count about 0.1°C) and chilled water flow; condenser water inlet and outlet temperatures and flow; and power input to the compressor, chilled water pump, condenser water pump and cooling tower fan.
explain: Flow can be read from an ultrasonic meter or inferred from pump duty. Design flows are about 0.68 m³/h per TR for chilled water and 0.91 m³/h per TR for condenser water.

front: What is the Integrated Part Load Value (IPLV), and which four load points does it use?
back: IPLV is a part-load efficiency reference using 100%, 75%, 50% and 25% of capacity, each given equal weight.
explain: The book calls IPLV the most appropriate reference, though not the best, because equal weighting ignores that equipment usually runs at 50–75% of capacity. Full-load kW/TR reflects design conditions that may occur only about 1% of the time.

front: What is the cooling load in TR for a medium-size office of 1000 m² with central air conditioning?
back: About 60 TR, using the indicative load of 0.06 TR/m².
explain: The book's profile is indicative only. A real design needs a detailed heat load calculation that includes people, lighting, envelope and air ingress.

front: With R-22, how much extra energy does an air-cooled condenser need compared with a water-cooled shell-and-tube condenser?
back: About 30% more. The air-cooled condenser ran at about 20 kg/cm² discharge pressure against about 15 kg/cm² for the water-cooled one.
explain: Higher discharge pressure adds compression work. The book recommends generously sized shell-and-tube water-cooled condensers (about 0.65 m² per TR and above) at the design stage.

front: By roughly how much does compressor power change for each 1°C rise in evaporator temperature?
back: It falls by about 3%. The same machine also gains TR capacity as evaporator temperature rises.
explain: A higher evaporator temperature raises suction pressure, which cuts the work of compression. The book advises the highest evaporator temperature the process can accept, with heat transfer areas sized to keep the driving temperature difference small.

front: How much extra energy can a 0.8 mm scale build-up on condenser tubes cause?
back: Up to about 35% more energy consumption.
explain: Fouled condenser tubes force the compressor to work harder for the same capacity. Fouled evaporators from residual lubricating oil or air infiltration also raise power use, so regular cleaning is a standard saving.

front: What is the difference between a cascade system and a compound (two-stage) system, and which applies at -46°C to -101°C?
back: Compound systems use one refrigerant with two compressors sharing the work of compression, used roughly from -20°C to -58°C. Cascade systems connect two separate systems with different refrigerants, one rejecting heat to the other, and are preferred for -46°C to -101°C.
explain: In a cascade, a low-temperature refrigerant with high suction temperature and low specific volume can be chosen for the low stage. Two compressors with low compression ratios together give a high overall ratio in a compound system.

front: Why is it more efficient to run one chiller at full load than two at part load?
back: Part-load operation of a chiller bank is inefficient, so each compressor should be loaded to full capacity before the next one starts.
explain: Isolation valves should stop chilled water flowing through idle chillers. Valves on idle branch lines also cut pressure drop and pumping power.

front: What is the Energy Efficiency Ratio (EER) of an air conditioner, and which labelling programme uses this definition?
back: Cooling capacity in watts divided by power input in watts at full-load conditions. The BEE star labelling programme uses this definition.
explain: Air properties from the psychrometric chart give the delivered capacity, which is then compared with power drawn to get kW/TR and EER. EER in W/W is the same as kW/kW.

explain: The book's example is a 10 TR package unit running only one of its two 5 TR compressors at low load. The book's EER uses 4.3 kW shaft power at 90% motor efficiency, not the 4.71 kW input.

front: How much electricity does an electrically driven heat pump need to supply 100 kWh of heat?
back: About 20–40 kWh for building heating; many industrial heat pumps need only 3–10 kWh.
explain: A heat pump moves heat from air, ground, water or waste heat to a higher temperature. The heat delivered equals the heat extracted plus the drive energy supplied.

front: What do ice bank (thermal storage) systems do, and what do they save?
back: They make and store ice at night on cheap off-peak power, then use the cooling in the day. This cuts peak demand and operating cost. In partial storage the chiller can be 40–50% smaller.
explain: ICEBANK tanks range from about 45 to over 500 ton-hours. Extending the chiller's hours of operation gives the lowest possible average load.

front: How is the mass of water added to humidify air calculated?
back: m_w = v × ρ × (w_out − w_in), where v is air flow (m³/h), ρ is air density (kg/m³), w is specific humidity (kg/kg) and m_w is water added (kg/h).
explain: Specific humidity is the mass of moisture per kg of dry air. Air density varies with temperature; the book uses 1.184 kg/m³ at 25°C in its textile example.

front: An air washer in a textile plant humidifies 3000 m³/h of air at 25°C from 10% to 60% RH by spray water. Specific humidity rises from 0.002 to 0.0062 kg/kg. How much water is needed?
back: About 14.9 kg/h.
explain: Water is added without heat, so the air moves along a constant enthalpy line and only its moisture content rises. The formula is m_w = v × ρ × (w_out − w_in).

front: Name three energy saving measures for an air conditioning system.
back: Any three of: insulating all cold lines and vessels at economic thickness; minimising the air conditioning load (roof cooling, false ceilings, efficient lighting, pre-cooling fresh air, variable air volume, sun film); minimising process heat loads (flow optimisation, avoiding idle flows, frequent heat exchanger cleaning); regular plant maintenance; matching plant to load with variable speed drives.
explain: The book groups these into cold insulation, building envelope, building heat loads, process heat loads and plant-area measures. Naming the group along with the measure reads well in an exam answer.

front: How does ASME use the specific ratio to classify fans, blowers and compressors?
back: Specific ratio = discharge pressure ÷ suction pressure. Fans: up to 1.11. Blowers: 1.11 to 1.20. Compressors: more than 1.20.
explain: The specific ratio is the ASME basis for the split, not the pressure alone. Fans move air at low pressure rise, blowers develop more, and compressors go beyond a ratio of 1.20. The book's Table 5.1 also lists pressure rise in mmWg for each class.

front: Why are radial fans called the industrial workhorses of centrifugal fans?
back: They develop high static pressure (up to about 1400 mm WC) and handle heavily contaminated airstreams. Their simple design suits high temperatures and medium blade tip speeds.
explain: Simple construction makes radial fans tolerant of dust and heat. They are the default choice for hard duty, but their efficiency is lower than airfoil and backward-curved designs.

front: Why are backward-inclined fans called non-overloading?
back: Their power reaches a peak and then falls within the usable airflow range, so changes in static pressure do not overload the motor.
explain: Backward-inclined fans are also more efficient than forward-curved fans. Stable motor loading is the reason the book prefers them where pressure varies.

front: What does a vaneaxial fan add to a tubeaxial fan, and what is its typical pressure limit?
back: Guide vanes that straighten and direct the flow. Pressure up to about 500 mm WC. It is typically the most energy-efficient fan and should be used whenever possible.
explain: Straightening the flow makes static pressure less dependent on duct pressure. Vaneaxial fans are the book's first choice where the application allows.

front: What defines a positive-displacement blower, and where is it preferred?
back: Rotors trap air and push it through the housing, giving a near-constant volume whatever the system pressure. Up to about 1.25 kg/cm². Preferred where material may clog, since it can blow clogged material free.
explain: Centrifugal blowers lose flow as pressure rises, which suits steady-volume conveying poorly. Positive-displacement units turn slowly (about 3,600 rpm) and are often belt driven so speed can be changed.

front: What are the peak efficiency ranges for airfoil/backward-curved, vaneaxial, tubeaxial and propeller fans?
back: Airfoil / backward-curved: 79-83%. Vaneaxial: 78-85%. Tubeaxial: 67-72%. Propeller: 45-50%.
explain: Axial-flow designs with guide vanes and aerofoil-type centrifugal blades sit at the top of the book's table. Use these ranges as a first check against manufacturer data, not as a substitute for it.

front: How much more efficient can aerofoil centrifugal blades be than backward-curved blades, and what limits their use?
back: Up to about 10% higher efficiency than backward-curved blades. Their use is limited to clean, dust-free air.
explain: Aerofoil blades are the most efficient centrifugal design, but dust erodes and disturbs them. That is why they suit clean-air duty only.

front: What is the operating point of a fan in a system?
back: The intersection of the system curve with the fan's static pressure curve. A vertical line from it to the power curve gives the power required.
explain: The actual flow and pressure are set by system resistance, not by the fan's nameplate alone. Changing the system resistance moves the operating point along the fan curve.

front: By how much do pressure and power rise if fan speed is increased by 10%?
back: Pressure rises by 21%. Power requirement rises by 33%.
explain: Pressure scales with speed squared and power with speed cubed: 1.1² = 1.21 and 1.1³ = 1.33. Flow rises by 10% with speed.

front: What safety margin on flow is generally allowed over the maximum process requirement?
back: About 5% over the maximum flow requirement, agreed with the process equipment supplier.
explain: Safety margins should be set with the process supplier, not as a default. The book warns that large margins produce oversized fans that run far below design flow at poor efficiency.

front: What safety margins does the book give for boiler induced-draft (ID) fans?
back: 20% on volume and 30% on head (pressure).
explain: ID fans are sized with larger margins than forced-draft and primary-air fans. The book's margins for FD and PA fans are smaller.

front: What are the consequences of oversizing a fan and letting it run far below its design flow?
back: It operates at very poor efficiency. Conservative safety margins are the usual cause.
explain: A fan's efficiency is best near its design flow. Oversizing pushes it to the low-flow end of its curve, wasting energy and capital.

front: Name five items the user should specify to a fan manufacturer for correct selection.
back: Any five of: design operating point (volume and pressure); normal operating point; maximum continuous rating; low-load operation; minimum and maximum ambient temperature. Others: gas temperature and density, gas composition, dust concentration and nature, control method, supply frequency, altitude.
explain: Low-load needs are specified separately when the plant will grow later. Ambient temperature and gas composition set the impeller's material of construction.

front: Why must system resistance be checked periodically?
back: Changes such as duct coatings, lining erosion, or equipment swaps (for example, multi-cyclones replaced by an ESP) can shift the operating point and cut fan efficiency.
explain: Coatings and erosion change resistance only marginally. A major equipment change can drastically move the operating point, so the fan may need replacing to keep its earlier efficiency.

front: What are the limits of damper control for fan flow?
back: Dampers add system resistance to change airflow, but they give limited adjustment and are not energy efficient.
explain: Damper control moves the operating point along the fan curve without changing speed. The book notes dampers are often left at an intermediate position because they are inconvenient to adjust.

front: How far can inlet guide vanes reduce flow while staying energy efficient?
back: From 100% flow down to about 80%. Below 80% flow, energy efficiency drops sharply.
explain: Guide vanes pre-swirl the air entering the fan, changing its fan curve. They suit modest flow reductions only.

front: How do variable-pitch axial fan blades save energy?
back: Blade pitch is changed hydraulically or pneumatically while the fan is running, which substantially modifies the fan characteristic. The book says this gives dramatically higher energy efficiency than the other options it discusses.
explain: Variable-pitch blades apply to axial-flow fans only. They are ranked above damper and guide-vane options in the book.

front: What is the turn-down ratio of a flow control method, and what limits it?
back: Turn-down ratio = maximum flow ÷ minimum flow. It is limited by leakage (slip) through dampers or vanes, by the control system for variable-speed drives, or by the fan's own characteristics.
explain: Even with dampers fully closed, leakage keeps the flow above zero. Stable fan operation needs the system curve to have a positive slope and the fan curve a negative slope.

front: What is the relationship between total, static and velocity pressure?
back: Total pressure (TP) = static pressure (SP) + velocity pressure (VP), so VP = TP − SP.
explain: Static pressure is the potential energy the fan puts into the system; it is given up to friction and converted to velocity pressure at the duct inlet. Velocity pressure is what you use to calculate air velocity.

front: Where and how should air velocity be measured in a duct?
back: In a straight duct at least 3-5 diameters downstream of elbows, branch entries or size changes. Take several traverse readings across the section, preferably on both suction and discharge sides.
explain: Bends and size changes distort the velocity profile, so readings taken close to them are unreliable. Traverse points on a circular duct are set at fixed concentric areas.

front: Why average the velocities, not the velocity pressures, across a duct?
back: Velocity varies across the duct. Calculate velocity at each traverse point, then average the velocities. Do not average the velocity pressures.
explain: Velocity depends on the square root of velocity pressure, so averaging pressures gives a wrong mean. If a full traverse is impossible, the book's approximation is to measure at the centre and multiply the velocity by 0.9.

front: How does excess air in combustion affect fan power, and what should be done?
back: Excess air increases the FD and ID fan load. Minimising excess air reduces fan power.
explain: Every extra unit of air the boiler or furnace takes in is air the fans must move. This is a demand-side measure that cuts fan power at the source.

front: Why are cold air in-leaks into a hot flue gas path so damaging to the ID fan?
back: Cold air increases the density of the flue gases and so the ID fan load. It can choke the fan's capacity and become a bottleneck for the boiler or furnace.
explain: The density increase raises the fan's power demand for the same gas handling. The book stresses that in-leaks must be minimised in kilns, boilers and furnaces.

front: Name five fan retrofit options for energy saving.
back: Any five of: high-efficiency impeller with cone; higher-efficiency fan assembly; impeller derating (smaller diameter); hollow FRP aerofoil impeller for axial fans; fan speed reduction by pulley change; two-speed motor or VSD for variable duty; energy-efficient flat or cogged belts; inlet guide vanes in place of discharge damper; duct system improvements.
explain: Several options cut the fan's duty, others cut transmission losses. The book lists nine options in total.

front: What did a variable-speed drive on the ID and FD fans of a 25 t/h boiler achieve?
back: Average power fell by nearly 41 kW, saving about Rs 0.33 million a year. The Rs 0.65 million VSD paid back in under 2 years.
explain: The boiler's fans were controlled by outlet dampers. A study of the airflow pattern showed a VSD would control flow much more efficiently.

front: What did a backward-curved impeller with erosion liners achieve at a cement plant's clinker cooler fans?
back: Power consumption fell by 53%, saving about Rs 2.1 million a year. The liners protect the blades from abrasive dust without frequent impeller changes.
explain: The old straight-blade impeller gave low system efficiency and the flow was higher than required. Replacing the impeller with a backward-curved blade, with liners against erosion, was a simple measure.

front: Why does parallel operation of two fans give less than double the flow in a typical system?
back: Two identical fans in parallel double the flow only at free delivery. The higher the system resistance, the smaller the flow gain.
explain: Parallel operation suits low-resistance systems that run close to free delivery. Series (push-pull) operation gives the most benefit in high-resistance systems.

back: About 3.9 kW (fan shaft about 3.5 kW).
explain: Airflow comes from room volume times air changes. The static efficiency formula gives fan shaft power, and motor efficiency gives the electrical input.

steps.explain: Length × breadth × height.
Convert air changes per hour to m³/s.
Rearranged static efficiency formula: kW = Q × SP ÷ (102 × η).
Motor input = shaft power ÷ motor efficiency.

front: A boiler ID fan is to be sized for 30,000 m³/h at 240 mm WC. Applying the book's ID fan safety margins, what is the design duty?
back: 36,000 m³/h at about 312 mm WC.
explain: The book gives ID fans a 20% margin on volume and a 30% margin on head. Margins are normally agreed with the process supplier.

steps.explain: 20% on volume for ID fans.
30% on head (pressure) for ID fans.
This is the duty to specify when sizing the ID fan.

front: A VSD for boiler fans costs Rs 0.65 million and saves Rs 0.33 million a year. What is the simple payback?
back: About 2.0 years (1.97). The book says it paid back in under 2 years.
explain: Simple payback is investment divided by annual saving. It ignores interest and inflation.

front: After a retrofit, a primary air fan's power falls from 57 kW to 22 kW. What is the percentage reduction?
back: About 61%.
explain: Percentage reduction is the drop divided by the original power. The book's case study gives these two values for the belt-driven to direct-coupled retrofit.

steps.answer: The retrofit changed a belt-driven arrangement to a direct-coupled fan with a more efficient impeller.
