front: What are the two basic types of reciprocating engines used to generate electricity?
back: Spark ignition (SI) engines and compression ignition (CI) engines.
explain: Spark ignition engines use a spark plug to ignite a compressed fuel-air mixture. Compression ignition engines compress air until it is hot enough to ignite injected fuel, and their higher compression ratio gives them higher efficiency.

front: Which fuels are typically used in spark ignition engines?
back: Gasoline, natural gas, and sewage and landfill gas.
explain: Spark ignition engines suit gaseous and light fuels that are mixed with air before combustion. Diesel and heavy fuel oil are normally used in compression ignition engines.

front: Which fuel is normally used in compression ignition engines, and how does a dual-fuel engine work?
back: Diesel or heavy fuel oil is normally used. In a dual-fuel engine, natural gas is compressed with the combustion air and diesel oil is injected at the top of the compression stroke to start combustion.
explain: The diesel oil acts as the ignition source for the gas-air mixture. The engine can therefore run mainly on natural gas while still using diesel to initiate combustion.

front: What compression ratio range is typical for a diesel engine, and what temperature does the compressed air reach?
back: 14:1 to 25:1. The air is heated to about 700-900°C, which ignites the injected diesel spontaneously.
explain: Because the fuel ignites from compression heat, the diesel engine is also called a compression ignition (CI) engine. The high compression ratio is why CI engines are more efficient than spark ignition engines.

front: Name the four strokes of a four-stroke diesel engine in order.
back: Induction, compression, ignition and power, exhaust.
explain: On induction the descending piston draws in fresh air. During compression the valves are closed and the air is compressed to up to 25 bar. Fuel is injected and ignites on the power stroke, and the exhaust stroke discharges the spent gases.

front: What is the approximate electrical efficiency of a modern lean-burn spark ignition gas engine?
back: Close to 45%.
explain: In a lean-burn gas engine, gas is mixed with air before the inlet valves, and a small prechamber with a richer mixture is ignited by a spark plug. Flames from the prechamber nozzle ignite the lean mixture in the main cylinder, so combustion is fast.

front: List the five components that make a diesel generating set a system.
back: (a) Diesel engine and accessories, (b) AC generator, (c) control systems and switchgear, (d) foundation and power house civil works, (e) the connected load and its components such as heating, motor drives and lighting.
explain: The set performs well only when these components are well matched. The chapter asks that each component be chosen for highest efficiency and run near its optimum efficiency level.

front: By how much should the engine power rating exceed the end-use power demand?
explain: The margin stops the machine being overloaded when motors start, when some lighting switches on, or when wear raises power consumption. The engine should not be sized exactly at the demand.

front: What speed range do diesel engines typically run at, and where should an engine be run?
back: Typically 1300-3000 RPM. Run the engine as close as possible to its rated speed.
explain: Running at rated speed avoids poor efficiency and deposit build-up from incomplete combustion, which raises maintenance and running costs. Speed is measured at the output shaft, and fuel efficiency is greatest at one optimum speed.

front: What captive power output range do diesel engine plants most frequently cover?
back: Most frequently used sizes are 4 to 15 MW.
explain: Diesel plants dominate small captive (non-utility) power because diesel engines are more efficient than gas turbines and small steam turbines in this range. For continuous operation a low speed engine is more cost-effective than a high speed engine.

front: Give four advantages of a captive diesel power plant.
back: Any four of: low installation cost; short delivery and installation period; efficiency as high as 43-45%; better performance at part loads; minimum cooling water needs; short start-up time.
explain: Diesel plants also suit a range of fuels, from light distillates to residual fuel oils. They can use air cooled heat exchangers where water is scarce.

front: How has the specific fuel consumption of diesel engines changed since the 1970s?
back: It has fallen from about 220 g/kWh in the 1970s to about 160 g/kWh at present.
explain: Modern high efficiency turbochargers allow an exhaust gas driven turbine generator to add output. This lowers fuel consumption per kWh and raises overall thermal efficiency.

front: Can a gas turbine burn the poorest quality fuel oils as easily as a diesel engine can?
back: No. A diesel engine can burn the poorest quality fuel oils, while a gas turbine needs costly fuel treatment equipment to do so.
explain: This is a common exam trap. Slow speed dual fuel engines using high-pressure gas injection also give the same thermal efficiency and power output as a regular fuel oil engine.

front: What is the normally accepted definition of a high speed engine?
back: An engine running at 1500 rpm.
explain: High speed sets have been developed in India, while slow speed engines of higher capacity are often imported. Slow speed engines suit continuous use, and high speed engines suit intermittent use.

front: Which engine type has the longer period between overhauls, and what are the typical intervals?
back: The slow speed engine, at about 8000 hours. The high speed engine is about 3200 hours (typical manufacturer recommendations).
explain: Slow speed engines have lower BMEP, less wear and tear, a higher weight-to-power ratio and lower direct operating cost. These features make them suitable for continuous use.

front: A plant has a 650 kW connected load, a diversity factor of 0.54, a 70% set loading and 0.8 PF. What DG set rating in kVA is needed?
back: About 625 kVA (maximum demand 350 kW, set rating 500 kW).
explain: Diversity factor here is maximum demand divided by connected load. The set should run at about 70% loading, and the kW rating is converted to kVA using the power factor.

steps.prompt: Find the maximum demand from the connected load and diversity factor.
steps.answer: Maximum demand = 650 kW × 0.54 = 351 kW, taken as 350 kW.
steps.explain: The diversity factor is demand divided by connected load, so demand = connected load × factor.

steps.prompt: Find the set rating in kW for 70% loading.
steps.explain: The set is sized so that the demand is about 70% of its rating.

steps.prompt: Convert the kW rating to kVA at 0.8 PF.
steps.explain: Generators are specified in kVA, so the kW rating is divided by the power factor.

front: Why is one large DG set usually preferred over two or more smaller sets?
back: One large set is more economical in space, operation, maintenance and initial capital investment.
explain: Parallel sets have their own benefits. Only the power shortfall needs to be met, one set can be stopped while another carries at least 50% of the requirement, and one set can serve as 100% standby in low power-cut periods.

front: Which protections are recommended on all DG sets, and which relay is essential for parallel operation?
back: Short circuit, overload and earth fault protection, plus high temperature and low lube oil pressure cut-outs. A reverse power relay is essential when sets run in parallel.
explain: Full circuit protection may be uneconomical on small sets, but it is strongly recommended. The reverse power relay prevents one alternator from back feeding another.

front: What is the largest direct-on-line (DOL) motor a DG set can start, and what starting method raises that limit?
back: Roughly 50% of the DG set kVA rating in HP with DOL starting. Star-delta or auto-transformer starting raises the limit to about 75% of the kVA rating.
explain: DOL starting draws up to six times rated current for a few seconds, and the starting current should not exceed about 200% of alternator full load capacity. Voltage and frequency recover well before the motor reaches full speed.

front: What does the electricity rules require for earthing a DG set?
back: Two independent earths, one to the equipment body and one to the neutral.
explain: Two independent earths give adequate protection against earth faults. They also drain away any leakage potential from the equipment for safe working.

front: A 500 kVA DG set is to start the largest possible motor. What is the limit in HP with DOL starting, and with star-delta or auto-transformer starting?
back: About 250 HP with DOL starting, and about 375 HP with star-delta or auto-transformer starting.
explain: The chapter gives these as approximate guides for the largest motor the set can start. Reduced-voltage starting cuts the starting current, which allows a larger motor.

steps.prompt: State the rule for the largest motor started by DOL.
steps.answer: Largest DOL motor (HP) is about 50% of the DG set kVA rating.
steps.explain: This follows from the limit on starting current for the alternator.

steps.prompt: Apply the DOL rule to a 500 kVA set.
steps.explain: The result is an approximate limit, not an exact value.

steps.prompt: Apply the star-delta or auto-transformer rule.
steps.explain: Reduced-voltage starting lowers the starting current, so the largest motor can be about 75% of the kVA rating.

front: How long can a diesel engine run at 10% overload, and how long can an alternator take 50% overload?
back: Diesel engine: 10% overload for 1 hour in every 12 hours of operation. Alternator: 50% overload for 15 seconds.
explain: Overloads that look harmless on utility supply can damage a DG set, so the set should be selected so that overloads stay within these limits. Steady loads give the best performance.

front: What engine loading should be maintained for a DG set, and at what alternator loading is efficiency highest?
back: Engine loading should be kept above 50% (in kW or BHP). Alternators reach their highest efficiency at around 70% loading and above.
explain: Engine manufacturers publish fuel consumption curves against engine loading. The best operating point for both engine and alternator should be used to reach high efficiency.

front: In what order should loads be started on a DG set?
back: Start the load with the highest transient kVA first, then the others in descending order of starting kVA.
explain: The base load already running reduces the transient handling capacity. On AC generators it also increases the transient voltage dip, so careful sequencing gives better use of the set.

front: What power factor is an AC generator designed for, and what is the economical fix for a low load power factor?
back: 0.8 lagging. The economical option is to add power factor improvement capacitors rather than oversize the generator.
explain: A low power factor needs higher excitation current, which increases losses. Oversizing the alternator for a low PF lowers its operating efficiency and raises cost.

front: Which exhaust source is hotter, and what are the approximate exhaust and cooling water temperatures in a reciprocating engine?
back: Exhaust gas is at about 450°C, against about 100°C for the cooling water. Each provides about half of the useful thermal energy, but exhaust is more versatile.
explain: Exhaust is much hotter, so it can drive higher temperature uses. Heat can also be recovered from the lubricating oil, jacket water and charge air coolers.

front: What is the formula for the potential waste heat recovery (WHR) from a reciprocating engine?
back: Potential WHR (kcal/h) = kWh output per hour × 8 kg gas per kWh × 0.25 kcal/kg°C × (t − 180)°C, where t is the gas temperature after the turbocharger.
explain: The 8 kg/kWh gas flow and 0.25 kcal/kg°C specific heat are the chapter's standard values. The 180°C floor is the lowest allowed exit temperature, set to avoid acid dew point corrosion.

front: A 1100 kVA DG set runs at 800 kW with 480°C exhaust gas temperature. What is the potential waste heat recovery?
back: About 4,80,000 kcal/h (4.8 lakh kcal/h).
explain: The chapter uses 8 kg of gas per kWh, 0.25 kcal/kg°C, and a 180°C exit floor. The result is the potential only; the realisable recovery depends on the site.

steps.prompt: Find the average kWh generated per hour.
steps.explain: The kWh output per hour equals the load in kW for steady operation.
The chapter takes 8 kg of exhaust gas per kWh generated.

steps.prompt: Find the usable temperature drop down to the 180°C floor.
steps.explain: 180°C is the lowest exit temperature allowed to avoid acid dew point corrosion.
Heat = flow × specific heat × temperature drop.

front: What three factors affect waste heat recovery from DG set flue gases?
back: DG set loading and exhaust gas temperature; hours of operation; and back pressure on the DG set.
explain: Continuous operation makes waste heat recovery more cost-effective. The back pressure added by the heat recovery unit must also stay within limits.

front: What minimum sustained DG set loading gives a reasonable flue gas flow and temperature for heat recovery?
back: Over 60% of rating.
explain: Fluctuating or gross under-loading gives erratic flue gas flow and temperature at the heat recovery unit, which can cause cold end corrosion. At 60% load in the chapter's 5 MW example, the unit gets 325°C inlet and 180°C outlet.

front: What is trigeneration?
back: The simultaneous production of electricity, heat and cooling from one fuel input. In a DG set, waste heat boilers make steam and jacket cooling water runs vapour absorption machines (VAM) for air conditioning.
explain: Trigeneration optimises fuel utilisation from a diesel or gas engine. The economics depend on the waste heat boiler and VAM capacity matched to the cooling need.

front: How long is the standard shop-floor energy performance trial on a DG set, and how often are readings logged?
back: A 2 hour trial at a steady load, with readings logged every 15 minutes.
explain: Logged quantities include fuel consumption, amps, volts, PF, kW and kWh, intake air and cooling water temperatures, cylinder exhaust temperatures, turbocharger RPM, charge air pressure, and cooler and stack gas temperatures.

front: List five energy saving measures for DG sets.
back: Any five of: steady load with cold, dust free intake air; better air filtration; fuel storage and handling per manufacturer and oil company guidelines; frequent calibration of fuel injection pumps; following the maintenance checklist; avoiding load fluctuations, phase imbalance and harmonic loads; regular field trials.
explain: Steady loading and clean intake air protect efficiency. Frequent fuel injection pump calibration and regular trials help keep the set at its best operating point.

front: A 180 kVA, 0.8 PF DG set has a 210 BHP engine. With no derating, and with 5.66 kW of alternator losses and exciter power, what is the maximum PF at full load?
back: About 0.84 (151 kW available ÷ 180 kVA).
explain: Engine power must be converted to kW, and losses subtracted, before dividing by the kVA rating. Running at this PF avoids overloading the set.

steps.prompt: Convert the engine rating from BHP to kW.
Subtract the alternator losses and exciter power.
steps.explain: Only the power left after losses is available as load at the alternator output.

steps.prompt: Divide by the kVA rating to get the maximum PF.
steps.explain: PF = kW / kVA, so this is the highest PF at which full kVA can be delivered without overloading the engine.

front: A DG set at 600 kW with 450°C exhaust gas (8 kg gas/kWh, 0.25 kcal/kg°C) drops to 230°C after a heat recovery boiler. How much steam is raised at 3 kg/cm² (enthalpy 650.57 kcal/kg) from 80°C feedwater?
back: About 462.7 kg/h of steam (heat recovered 2,64,000 kcal/h).
explain: Steam output is the recovered heat divided by the heat added per kg of steam, which is the steam enthalpy minus the feedwater enthalpy. The chapter's method is used here.

steps.explain: The heat recovered is kWh per hour × gas per kWh × specific heat × temperature drop.

steps.prompt: Find the heat added per kg of steam.
steps.explain: The feedwater must be heated from 80°C before it becomes steam at the given enthalpy.

steps.prompt: Divide heat recovered by heat per kg.
steps.explain: This gives the steam generation rate.

front: A DG set at 750 kW with 440°C exhaust gas (8 kg gas/kWh, 0.25 kcal/kg°C) drops to 190°C after a heat recovery boiler. Steam enthalpy is 650 kcal/kg and feedwater is 70°C. How much steam is generated?
back: About 647 kg/h.
explain: This follows the same method as the chapter's worked example. The steam rate is the heat recovered divided by the enthalpy rise per kg of feedwater.

steps.explain: 8 kg of gas is generated per kWh.
The exhaust gas is cooled from 440°C to 190°C in the boiler.
Heat = flow × specific heat × temperature drop.
Heat per kg is the steam enthalpy minus the feedwater temperature.

front: A 6 MW furnace oil DG set averages 5 MW and burns 1230 litres/h at Rs 28/litre. What is the fuel cost of generation in Rs/kWh?
back: About Rs 6.89/kWh (furnace oil only).
explain: The chapter gives no gas fuel price, so only the furnace oil cost is computed. The answer is the fuel cost per kWh delivered at the average load.

steps.explain: Cost = litres per hour × price per litre.

steps.prompt: Find the energy generated per hour.
steps.explain: At steady average load, kWh per hour equals kW.
Divide hourly fuel cost by hourly energy generated.

front: How much energy does a 3.5 MW DG set generate in a year at 80% load factor for 7000 hours?
back: About 1.96 × 10⁷ kWh (19,600 MWh).
explain: Energy = rated kW × load factor × hours. The waste heat part of this question needs the exhaust temperature, which the chapter's question data does not give.

steps.prompt: Find the average load in kW.
steps.explain: The load factor is the average load as a fraction of the rated capacity.
Energy = average kW × operating hours.

front: What is the purpose of the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC)?
back: It sets the minimum energy efficiency standards for the design and construction of commercial buildings, encouraging efficient design or major retrofit without compromising building function, comfort, health or occupant productivity.
explain: ECBC is a code with minimum requirements, aimed at new commercial buildings and major retrofits. The chapter stresses that efficiency must not come at the cost of function, comfort or productivity.

front: Under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2010, what connected load or contract demand makes a commercial structure a ‘building’?
back: A connected load of 100 kW or more, or a contract demand of 120 kVA or more, used or intended for commercial purposes.
explain: The definition also covers existing structures that meet these ratings. Note that load is given in kW and contract demand in kVA, so the two thresholds are not interchangeable.

front: Name the five climatic zones into which India is divided for ECBC.
back: Composite, Hot Dry, Warm Humid, Moderate and Cold.
explain: The climate zone sets the climate-based prescriptive values for walls, roofs and windows, so the zone must be identified before choosing a compliance path. Figure 10.1 shows the zone map. ‘Cold-humid’ is not one of the five zones.

front: Which aspects of a building does the ECBC cover?
back: Building envelope (except unconditioned storage spaces or warehouses); mechanical systems including HVAC; service hot water; interior and exterior lighting; and electrical power and motors.
explain: These five areas are the subject of the code’s Chapters 4 to 8. The envelope rules do not apply to unconditioned storage spaces or warehouses.

front: What does the ECBC NOT apply to?
back: Buildings that use neither electricity nor fossil fuel, and equipment or building-system portions that use energy primarily for manufacturing processes.
explain: The exclusions depend on the energy source and on process use, not on building size. Process equipment in a factory is outside the code, but the building’s own HVAC and lighting are still covered.

front: Name the three ECBC compliance approaches for the building envelope.
back: Prescriptive approach, envelope trade-off approach, and Whole Building Performance (WBP) approach.
explain: The building must first meet all mandatory provisions. Prescriptive is quick but rigid, trade-off lets efficiency shift between roof, walls and windows, and WBP uses energy simulation and is the most flexible but needs the most effort.

front: How does the Whole Building Performance method show ECBC compliance?
back: The estimated annual energy use of the Proposed Design is compared with that of the Standard Design (the same building meeting all prescriptive requirements). Compliance requires the Proposed Design to use no more energy than the Standard Design.
explain: The Standard Design sets the upper limit of allowed energy use. The method needs approved simulation software (Appendix B of the Code) and close coordination across the design team.

front: Name five areas of the building envelope that must be sealed, caulked, gasketed or weather-stripped.
back: Joints around fenestration and door frames; openings between walls and foundations, roof or wall panels; openings where utility services penetrate roofs, walls or floors; site-built fenestration and doors; building assemblies used as ducts or plenums; and all other envelope openings.
explain: Air leakage through the envelope adds an infiltration load that the HVAC system must then condition. The chapter lists the areas as a to f, and any other opening in the envelope must also be sealed.

front: In a hot climate, how should buildings be oriented to limit solar gain?
back: Minimise exposure to the east and west, since these faces get the highest solar heat gain. The long sides of buildings should face north and south.
explain: Plot lines and roads should be laid out to limit east and west exposure. The chapter notes that good orientation can be achieved at no added cost when planned early.

front: What two properties define a cool roof, and what are the ECBC prescriptive minimum values?
back: High solar reflectance and high thermal emittance. Minimum solar reflectance 0.7 and initial emittance 0.75.
explain: A cool roof reflects sunlight and radiates absorbed heat back to the environment, so less heat passes into the building below. Values must be determined by the standards the code specifies.

front: What does visible light transmittance (VLT) measure, and why does it matter?
back: The fraction of visible light passing through glazing. It counts only the visible part of the solar spectrum, unlike SHGC, which counts all solar radiation.
explain: VLT is the key parameter for daylighting, because it shows how much usable light gets in. A window can have a low SHGC and a high VLT, which is the goal of spectral selectivity.

front: How is window-to-wall ratio (WWR) defined?
back: Vertical fenestration area divided by gross exterior wall area. Gross wall area is measured from the top of the floor to the bottom of the roof.
explain: WWR is used to select the fenestration requirement and to calculate effective aperture. Only vertical fenestration counts, so skylights are not included.

front: A building has a WWR of 0.4 and glazing with a VLT of 0.26. Does the glazing comply with ECBC by the effective aperture test (EA above 0.1)?
back: Yes. EA = 0.26 × 0.4 = 0.104, which is above 0.1, so the glazing complies.
explain: Effective aperture combines how much light the glazing passes with how much of the wall is glazed. Aperture size alone is not a good measure, because tinted or low-VLT glazing admits less light.

steps.explain: Light admitted depends on the glazing’s visible transmittance and on the glazed share of the wall.
Multiply the VLT by the window-to-wall ratio.

steps.prompt: Compare EA with the 0.1 test value.
steps.answer: 0.104 is above 0.1, so the glazing complies with ECBC.
steps.explain: The chapter’s worked example uses 0.1 as the pass mark.

front: A building has a WWR of 0.6 and glazing with a VLT of 0.15. Does it comply by the EA test (EA above 0.1)? What minimum VLT would pass at this WWR?
back: No. EA = 0.15 × 0.6 = 0.09, below 0.1. At WWR 0.6 the VLT must be at least about 0.17 (0.1 ÷ 0.6).
explain: A higher WWR means more glazing, so the glass must transmit more light per unit of wall area to keep EA up. The 0.17 figure is derived from the chapter’s 0.1 test value rather than stated in the text.

steps.explain: EA is the effective daylight opening after the glazing’s transmittance is applied.
Multiply the VLT by the window-to-wall ratio.

steps.answer: 0.09 is below 0.1, so the glazing does not comply.
steps.explain: Failing this test means the glazing or the glazed area must change.

steps.prompt: Find the minimum VLT at WWR 0.6.
steps.explain: Rearranging EA = VLT × WWR gives the required VLT for the same test value.

front: What are the ECBC maximum U-factor and SHGC limits for vertical fenestration in the Composite zone?
back: Maximum U-factor 3.30 W/m²·°C; maximum SHGC 0.25 where WWR is below 40%, and 0.20 where WWR is 40% to 60%.
explain: As the glazed share of the wall grows, the SHGC limit gets tighter. The OCR of Table 10.3 was partly broken, so check these values against the printed table before relying on them.

front: What is the ECBC limit on skylight area under the prescriptive approach?
back: Skylight area is limited to a maximum of 5% of the gross roof area. Skylights must also meet maximum U-factor and SHGC values.
explain: The cap stops daylight gain from becoming excess heat and glare. This is the prescriptive skylight requirement in ECBC 4.3.4.

front: Which building components can be traded off against each other under the envelope trade-off approach, and what must be shown?
back: Trade-offs are allowed only among the major envelope components: roof, walls and fenestration. The proposed design’s Envelope Performance Factor (EPF) must be equal to or better than the baseline design’s EPF.
explain: EPF is calculated using Appendix D of the ECBC. Trade-offs cannot cross into HVAC or lighting; those systems have their own requirements.

front: What HVAC controls does ECBC require for equipment above 28 kW cooling or 7 kW heating?
back: A time clock that keeps its programme for at least 10 hours and controls varying schedules. Each zone needs its own temperature controller, heating-and-cooling equipment needs a 3 °C (5 °F) dead band, and thermostats must prevent simultaneous heating and cooling.
explain: The time clock lets equipment run only when it is needed. The dead band keeps the heating and cooling set points apart so one does not fight the other.

front: True or false: spiral lock joints in round and flat oval ducts must be sealed.
back: False. Spiral lock joints need not be sealed. Longitudinal seams and transverse joints do need sealing.
explain: Leaks let conditioned air escape to unconditioned spaces or outdoors. The chapter calls duct sealing one of the most important conservation checks, and ducts in unconditioned spaces also need insulation.

front: Which hydronic pumps must have variable speed drives under ECBC, and what flow range must they allow?
back: Pump motors of 3.7 kW (5 HP) and above in all hydronic systems must have variable speed drives. Pump flow must be controllable down to 50% of design, or the manufacturer’s minimum for the chiller or boiler.
explain: Throttling keeps the motor at full speed and wastes energy. A variable speed drive lowers the motor speed and power while still delivering the required flow.

front: When does ECBC require an economizer on a cooling system?
back: When the fan capacity is above 1,200 L/s (2,500 cfm) and the cooling capacity is above 22 kW.
explain: An economizer cools with outside air when temperature and humidity are mild, instead of running refrigeration on recirculated air. A properly operating economizer can cut a building’s total energy use by as much as 10%.

front: For residential facilities, hotels and hospitals with a centralised system, what share of design capacity must come from solar water heating?
back: At least 20% of the design capacity.
explain: Supplementary heating must be cascaded: heat recovery from hot discharge (such as AC condensers) first, then gas-fired heaters where gas is available, and an electric heater only as a last resort.

front: A hotel has four floors of 1000 m² each. If the LPD is 10.8 W/m², what is the interior lighting power allowance by the building area method?
explain: Under the building area method, the allowance is the sum of gross lighted floor area times the allowed LPD for each building area type. The four floors here are treated as one type, so the total area is multiplied by the LPD.

steps.prompt: Find the total gross lighted floor area.
steps.explain: The building area method uses the gross lighted floor area of each building area type.

steps.prompt: Multiply the total area by the LPD.
steps.explain: Allowance in watts equals area times the allowed watts per square metre.

steps.answer: 43,200 W = 43.2 kW, the interior lighting power allowance.
steps.explain: The installed interior lighting load is compared with this allowance to check compliance.

front: An enclosed office has an area of 400 m². If the LPD is 11.8 W/m², what is its interior lighting power allowance by the space function method?
explain: Under the space function method, the building allowance is the sum of the allowances for all spaces, and each space’s allowance is its gross lighted floor area times the LPD for that space type.

steps.prompt: Identify the method and its rule.
steps.answer: Space function method: each space gets area × LPD for its type, and the building total is the sum over all spaces.
steps.explain: This method suits buildings with mixed space types, such as offices, corridors and storage.
Use the gross lighted floor area of the enclosed office.

steps.answer: Add the allowance of every other space to 4720 W to get the building allowance.
steps.explain: The office figure is one term in the sum over all spaces.

front: What is the ECBC rule for exit signs?
back: An internally-illuminated exit sign must not exceed 5 W per face.
explain: An exit sign is lit continuously, so its wattage per face adds up over the building’s life. The chapter also suggests changing exit signs from incandescent to LED.

front: What lamp efficacy does ECBC require for exterior grounds luminaires above 100 W, and what exception applies?
back: A minimum efficacy of 60 lm/W, unless the luminaire is controlled by a motion sensor.
explain: Exterior lighting must also be controlled by a photo sensor or an astronomical time switch that turns it off when daylight is available or the light is not needed.

front: What power factor must a 3-phase electricity supply above 100 A maintain under ECBC?
back: Between 0.95 lagging and unity, at the point of connection.
explain: Supplies above 1,000 kVA also need permanent metering of demand (kVA), energy (kWh) and total power factor. Supplies between 65 and 1,000 kVA need demand (kW), energy and power factor (or kVARh) metering.

front: Name four energy conservation measures for building water pumping systems.
back: High-efficiency pumps; operating pumps in parallel; automatic operation with low-level/high-level flow control; and variable frequency drives on chilled water and cooling water pumps.
explain: Building pumps are usually centrifugal at about 60% efficiency, so efficiency upgrades and drives are the main levers. Pumps serve chilled water, cooling water, domestic water, hot water and sewage.

front: Name the four main components of a UPS and state what the inverter does.
back: Converter (AC to DC), battery, inverter (DC to AC), and monitor and control hardware and software. The inverter converts DC to AC.
explain: The charger and converter bring utility AC to DC for the battery. The inverter then rebuilds AC for the load when the battery supplies power.

front: What are the two UPS architectures, and which one is more efficient?
back: Off-line (line-interactive) and on-line (double-conversion). The off-line type is more efficient because the load connects directly to the AC input.
explain: A line-interactive UPS uses an auto-transformer AVR to correct small voltage deviations. On an unstable grid, its frequent switches to battery shorten battery life, while the on-line type gives a clean, stable sine-wave output.

front: At what load range do most UPS systems operate, and at what load range should their efficiency be demonstrated?
back: Most operate at 25% to 60% of nominal load. Efficiency should be shown at 25% to 50% load.
explain: Most UPSs peak in efficiency between 50% and 100% load, so a full-load figure overstates real performance. Most computer and server loads are non-linear, which also lowers UPS efficiency.

front: A UPS draws 100 kW from the utility and delivers 90 kW to the critical loads, with the difference lost as heat in conversion. What is its efficiency?
explain: UPS efficiency is the useful energy out divided by the energy in. The conversion loss is the difference between the two, and it is released as heat.

steps.prompt: Identify the input and the useful output.
steps.explain: Efficiency compares energy that reaches the loads with energy drawn from the utility.

steps.answer: 100 kW − 90 kW = 10 kW lost as heat.
steps.explain: The loss happens in the transformers, rectifiers and inverters inside the UPS.
Efficiency is output divided by input.

steps.answer: A figure at full load may overstate performance, since most UPS run at 25% to 60% load. Test at 25% to 50% load.
steps.explain: The chapter asks for efficiency at the loads where UPSs usually operate.

front: What power is measured to assess the energy performance of a lift, and what is measured for an escalator?
back: Lift: power at rated load moving upward at contract speed. Escalator or passenger conveyor: power with no load, running at rated speed (up or down).
explain: An escalator’s rated load is given as a number of persons, not in kg, so there is no theoretical rated load to test with. The no-load running power shows the fixed friction overhead.

front: What are the four categories of energy consumed by lifts and escalators?
back: Friction losses while travelling; dynamic losses during starting and stopping; lifting (or lowering) work, i.e. potential energy transfer; and regeneration into the supply system.
explain: The general approach to efficiency is to minimise friction and dynamic losses. Specifying efficient equipment, avoiding over-design and zoning the lift system are the main principles.

front: What is the function of a building management system (BMS or BEMS)?
back: Monitoring and control of a building’s services and functions in a way that is economical and efficient in energy use. One system can also control a group of buildings.
explain: BEMS ranges from a simple timer for on and off schedules to a computerised central controller fed by sensors. The chapter notes that good results need proper design, installation and commissioning.

front: How does the national star rating for office buildings work, and what does 5 star mean?
back: Buildings are rated on a 1 to 5 star scale based on specific energy use in kWh/m²/yr. 5 star is the most efficient. A label is valid for 5 years from the date of issue.
explain: The rating normalises for operating hours, climate zone and conditioned space, and compares a building with its peer group. It acts as an external benchmark that helps owners find buildings with the best opportunities for improvement.

front: In the New Delhi (composite zone) example, what EPI gives a 5-star rating, and what is the 1-star band?
back: An EPI below 90 kWh/m²/yr gives 5 stars, for a building with more than 50% air-conditioned area. The 1-star band is 165 to 190 kWh/m²/yr.
explain: The EPI bandwidth depends on the climate zone and the air-conditioned share of the built-up area. New Delhi is the chapter’s worked example for the composite zone.

front: A BPO building has an EPI of 150 kWh/m²/yr. It operates 8 hours a day, 5 days a week. What is its AAhEPI in (Wh/m²)/hr?
back: About 72.1 (Wh/m²)/hr.
explain: AAhEPI converts an annual energy index into an hourly index, so BPO buildings with different operating hours can be compared on one scale. The formula uses 52 weeks to convert the weekly schedule to a year.

steps.explain: The 52 converts the weekly schedule into annual operating hours.
Multiply daily hours, days per week and weeks per year.

steps.prompt: Divide the EPI by the operating hours.
steps.explain: This gives the average hourly energy per square metre.
The ×1000 converts kWh to Wh, which is the AAhEPI unit.

front: What unit is AAhEPI given in for BPO buildings, and what is excluded from its electricity total?
back: (Wh/m²)/hr. Electricity generated from on-site renewable sources, such as solar PV, is excluded from the total.
explain: AAhEPI uses purchased and generated electricity divided by built-up area and total annual operating hours. The result does not depend on time of day, so it applies to all BPO operations.

front: What temperature and relative humidity does the chapter recommend for comfort in air-conditioned spaces?
back: Temperature between 23 °C and 25 °C, and relative humidity between 55% and 65%.
explain: The chapter gives these as the comfort setpoints for air-conditioned spaces. Holding them, rather than cooling further, is the basis of the AC measures that follow in the same section.

front: What saving do compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) give over incandescent bulbs?
back: About 75% less electricity, with no reduction in illumination levels.
explain: A lamp’s lighting efficacy (lumens per watt) decides how many watts a given light output needs. CFLs are the chapter’s example of a high-efficiency replacement for incandescent lamps.

front: Above what floor area must interior lighting have an automatic control device, and when must occupancy sensors switch lights off?
back: Buildings larger than 500 m² (5,000 ft²). Occupancy sensors must turn lights off within 30 minutes of an occupant leaving the space.
explain: Office areas below 30 m², meeting and conference rooms, school classrooms and storage spaces must have occupancy sensors. Other spaces can use scheduled control, with independent schedules for areas up to 2,500 m² on one floor.

front: A plant has 200 fluorescent fittings. Conventional ballasts lose 12 W each and electronic ballasts lose 2 W each. How much power is saved by replacing all of them?
explain: Ballast losses add to the lamp power of every fitting, so each electronic ballast saves 10 W. Across many fittings this adds up quickly, and the saving is a continuous reduction in electricity draw.

steps.explain: Compare the loss of the conventional ballast with that of the electronic one.

steps.prompt: Multiply by the number of fittings.
steps.explain: Each fitting makes the same saving.
This is the reduction in connected load.
The 6000 h/yr operating time is an assumed example, not a value from the chapter.

front: A compressor draws 100 kW at 8 kg/cm² discharge pressure. Reducing discharge pressure to 7 kg/cm² saves how much power, by the chapter rule of thumb?
back: About 9%, which is about 9 kW. Compressed-air leakage also falls by about 10%.
explain: Each 1 kg/cm² of pressure reduction cuts input power, and it also cuts leakage, since leak rates rise with pressure. The chapter advises setting discharge pressure to the lowest acceptable value.

steps.answer: Reducing air pressure by 1 kg/cm² (8 to 7) saves 9% of input power.
steps.explain: This is the chapter’s compressed-air rule of thumb.
Apply the percentage to the compressor’s input power.
Lower pressure means less air escapes through leaks, so less air must be compressed.

front: A chiller compressor draws 200 kW. Lowering the condensing temperature by 5.5 °C cuts compressor power by 20% to 25%. What is the saving, and what is the new compressor power?
back: A saving of 40 to 50 kW, so the compressor draws about 150 to 160 kW.
explain: Cooler condenser water lowers the pressure the compressor must work against, so less work is needed. The chapter also advises using the lowest-temperature condenser water the chiller can handle.

steps.answer: Reducing condensing temperature by 5.5 °C reduces compressor power by 20% to 25%.
steps.explain: This is a rule of thumb from the chapter’s chiller checklist.
Use the low end of the range for a conservative figure.
Use the high end of the range for an optimistic figure.
Subtract each saving from the original 200 kW draw.
